blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
There is an age — I would put it at somewhere between fifteen and twenty-four, though it varies and some people never leave it — at which a young man will accept a story as a set of instructions.
Not as a story. Not as a shape somebody made to hold something that has no shape of its own. As instructions. As a map with a legend, drawn to scale, of a country he is actually standing in.

I was that age once and I was extremely good at it. I could take a thing that had been polished by thirteen hundred years of being told in the dark by men who wanted you to weep, and I could hold it up against my own street, my own week, my own small stupid griefs, and find the correspondences. And I found them. That is the thing nobody warns you about. You always find them. A story that has survived that long has survived precisely because it fits everything, and a thing that fits everything is not a key, it is a blindfold with a very beautiful pattern printed on it.
I want to be careful here, because there is a lazy version of this book and I did not want to write it.

The lazy version says the old stories are lies and the people who keep them are fools. That is not true and it is not interesting and anybody who has actually stood in one of those rooms knows it is not true. What happens in those rooms is real. The grief is real, the food is real, the arms around you when your legs go are real, and the thing that happens to a human nervous system after ten nights of no sleep and no food and a fixed beat is so real that it can be measured with a stopwatch and I have put the number in the book.
The danger was never the story.
The danger is the moment a person stops reading it as a story and starts using it as an address.

Everything that goes wrong in this book goes wrong because somebody looked at a thing in front of him — a stain, a boy, an alley, a night, another man’s death — and reached for the oldest, largest, most beautiful explanation available instead of the small ugly one that was true. Every land is Karbala. It is the finest sentence we have. It is also, if you hand it to a frightened child at the wrong moment, a way of making sure he never asks the second question.

I have watched men do this with epics and I have watched men do it with politics and I have watched men do it with their own families, and it is always the same move, and it is always made by somebody who loves you.

The people in these pages are not fanatics. I have no interest in fanatics. They are ordinary, competent, generous people who are extremely serious about something that was never meant to be taken that seriously, and who are, for the most part, kind — and the kindness is the mechanism, not the exception. A cage built by people who do not love you is easy to leave.
I got out of mine late, at some cost, in another country, and I would like to say I did it by being clever. I did not. Somebody paid for the ticket.

The history in this book is accurate. I have checked it more carefully than I have checked most things in my life. The names, the days, the water, the eight hundred kilometres, the woman in the court who would not stop talking — all of that happened, or is believed to have happened by enough people for long enough that the difference has stopped being useful.
What I have added is one boy, one alley, and eleven minutes.

Read the old parts as history. Read the new parts as a warning. And if you find yourself, at any point, noticing how exactly the ancient thing maps onto your own life — put the book down for a minute. That feeling is the subject.
Chew Z
THE PARDEH
PART ONE — BEFORE
1. THE NIGHT — blue
I have let you assume something for a long time and it is time I stopped.
I was not a boy from Nazi Abad [naa-ZEE aa-BAAD].

I want to be exact about this because the exactness is the whole of it. In the year 1382 I lived in a four-bedroom apartment on the eighth floor of a building in Elahieh [e-laa-hee-YEH], in the north of Tehran, with a doorman and an underground car park and a view down the length of the city on the four days a year you could see the length of the city.

My mother taught art history. My father was, and is, an engineer, and put the lifts into the towers that my other grandfather’s firm put up. There was a Steinway in that apartment that nobody played. There was wine in the kitchen in a cupboard that did not lock, in a country where that is a serious matter, and it was there because it had always been there and because nobody in my family had ever seriously entertained the idea that anyone would come.
Nobody in that apartment prayed. Not once, not ever, not at a funeral. My grandmother could not have told you which way was Mecca from her own living room and would have found the question amusing.

And in the last days of Zilhajjeh, 1382, on the edge of Muharram [mo-har-RAM], I got on the number 130 with a bag and went forty minutes south to a walled yard behind a butcher’s shop and beat myself with a chain until I bled through my shirt.
Now. Here is my family, so that you understand what I was doing.

My grandfather on my mother’s side, Yousef [yoo-SEF], was born in 1309 and founded, out of nothing, a firm that put up a fair fraction of the towers in the north of this city, and was, in the plainest and most complete sense of the word, a Persepolis [per-se-PO-lis] man.

Persepolis — Perspolis, as everyone here says it — is one of the two great football clubs of this country. Red. Founded in 1342. And in the south and the centre and the bazaar and in every taxi in this city, red is not a preference, it is a category of person.

My grandfather went to the Azadi [aa-zaa-DEE] stadium for thirty years and did not stop going when his knees went. He had a red scarf that was older than my mother and had been washed so many times it was the colour of a brick left out in weather.

His other son-in-law — the husband of my aunt Soraya [so-ra-YAA] — is a man I am not going to name in a published book, and he played for that club in the nineteen-seventies, and he was, for about four seasons, genuinely and nationally famous.

He came to lunch. He came to lunch constantly. There is a photograph of me at six years old sitting on the knee of a man whose face was on the side of buildings, wearing a red shirt that had been bought for me before I could walk.

And my brother Amir [a-MEER], who is four years older than me and who has never in his life done a single thing that surprised anybody, wore red from the day he could dress himself and wears it now, in Toronto, at thirty-eight, in a house with a mortgage.
I supported Esteghlal [es-tegh-LAAL].
Blue. The other one. The one you support if you want every meal in my grandfather’s house to become an event.

And I need to tell you when I made that decision, because the date is the point. I was seven. I did not watch a match and fall in love with a player. I did not have a friend who took me. I have gone back over it honestly, as an adult, in a country where nobody cares, and the truth is exactly as small as it sounds:
I worked out, at seven years old, that there was one thing in that apartment that everybody agreed about, and that if I stopped agreeing about it, I would be a person.

That is it. That is the entire origin. It is not a good story and I have told the good story at parties for years — the aunt’s husband, the derby, the grandfather’s scarf — and none of the good story is the reason.
And here is the thing I did not see until I was about thirty, sitting in an office in another country being asked, professionally, to describe my own history in chronological order.
Esteghlal means independence.
I chose the club whose name is the word for the thing I thought I was doing, and I have spent my entire adult life discovering that I have never once in my life been independent of anything.
The football came first and the rest of it followed the same road.
At nine my grandfather died — my father’s father, the one from the south, the one I will get to. I stopped speaking for six weeks — that part is true and I have not exaggerated it.

And my mother, who is an intelligent and loving woman and who was thirty-nine years old and had a husband who had gone quiet in the same month as his son, in a manner nobody in that apartment would name, did what people of our sort do. Two psychologists. A paediatrician in Jordan Street. A month at her sister’s. All of it correct and all of it well-intentioned and none of it worked.

And in Farvardin [far-var-DEEN] of 1377 my uncle Mehran [meh-RAAN] — her younger brother, the one who had gone to the war at nineteen when the rest of the family had arranged things so that nobody had to, the one whose lungs were the family’s permanent quiet embarrassment, the one who lived in two rooms in Nazi Abad because he had refused everything anyone tried to give him — my uncle Mehran came up to Elahieh and said: let me take him south for a week.
And my mother, who had run out of everything else, said yes.
I came back talking.

She has never forgiven any of it. Not him, not the yard, not Nemat [ne-MAT], not me. She said something to me at seventeen, in a kitchen, that I am not going to repeat, about what she had handed over and what came back.
She was not wrong. That is the thing about my mother. She has been right about all of it from the first week.
So by fifteen I had been going down there for six years and it had become the fixed and central fact of my life, and my family’s relationship to it can be described precisely.
Amir thought it was a phase and told his friends about it as a funny thing his younger brother did, in the tone you would use about a brother who had got into heavy metal.
My aunt Soraya thought it was dangerous and said so once a year.
My grandfather thought it was, and I quote him exactly, because he said it at a table with eleven people at it: at least it is not the blue lot.

My mother knew exactly what it was and could not say so out loud, because the thing she would have had to say was: my son found a room full of men where nobody asks him anything, six months after his grandfather, and I have nothing at home that competes with that.
Nobody in that yard knew where I lived.
Nobody. Not for six years.

I got off the bus two stops early and walked in. I owned one set of clothes for it and they lived at Mehran’s. My accent went south the moment I came through the passage and I did not do that on purpose, it happened, the way it happens to everybody, and by fifteen I had two accents and used them in two halves of one city and did not consider this remarkable.

Haj Nemat knew. Agha Sadegh [SAA-degh] knew. They had known since the first year and they never once said it in front of anybody, and I did not understand until I was twenty-two that this was the single largest favour any human being has ever done me.
I thought I was passing.

Three hundred and forty men in a walled yard, and I thought I was passing, and every single one of them had clocked me by the second night of the first year, because you can change a coat and you cannot change how a boy holds a tea glass.
They let me have it.
That is the sentence. That is what those men did, for six years, without a meeting and without a discussion and without one of them ever saying a word to me about it.

A rich boy from the north came down on a bus wanting to be somebody else, and three hundred and forty men from the south of this city looked at him and decided, collectively and silently, to let him have it.
And they gave him the front row, and a light chain, and the part of Abbas [ab-BAAS], and a tempo.
I have spent nineteen years trying to decide what that was.

I have got as far as this: it was the most generous thing I have ever been given, and it was a costume, and both of those are true, and I still do not know whether the men who gave it to me were being kind to a grieving child or were quietly and enormously amused, and the answer is almost certainly that it was both at once and that this is what people are.
2. THE NIGHT — the other son

My father is Kamran [kam-RAAN] Shabani [sha-baa-NEE] and my mother is Layla [LEY-laa], and I have never once been able to say her name in a room with my uncle in it without thinking about the marshes.

Because the field where they fed nineteen-year-olds for eight years was called Majnoon [maj-NOON], and majnoon is the word for a man who has lost his mind, and the reason it is that word is the old poem — the boy who loved a girl so completely that he went into the desert and forgot how to be a person, and his name is Majnoon and her name is Leyli [ley-LEE].
My uncle went to Majnoon.
His sister is called Layla.
There is nothing in that. It is a coincidence and it means nothing and there are four hundred thousand women in this country with that name. I have known it was nothing since I was about nineteen.
I have never once stopped noticing it.
My brother is Amir and he is four years older than me and there was nothing wrong with him at all.
I mean that as a description and not as an insult, although it took me until about twenty-eight to be able to say it without it being one.

He was handsome in the way that is not a matter of opinion. Tall by fourteen. He had our mother’s face, which is a good face, and he had a way of coming into a room that I have watched carefully for thirty years and never once been able to reproduce, which is that he came in as though the room had been waiting for him and he was slightly sorry to have kept it.
He was good at football. He was not brilliant at it and he did not need to be, because he was good at it in the way that gets you picked, which is more useful.
He was funny. That is the one I cannot get around. He was actually funny, at fifteen, in a way that adults laughed at rather than encouraged.

Our grandfather adored him. Our aunt adored him. The famous footballer who came to lunch talked to Amir and was pleasant to me, and there is a photograph from Nowruz [now-ROOZ] 1375 in which Amir is between the two of them with his arms round both and I am at the end of the row looking at something outside the frame.
I have that photograph. I brought it eleven thousand kilometres. I do not know why.
And I was the other one.

I was small until I was fourteen and then I went up all at once, which is its own separate problem. And I frowned. That is not self-deprecation, it is a documented family position, and my father’s father made a joke of it that lasted my whole childhood.
He called me Boloor [bo-LOOR].
It means crystal. The good kind, the kind that catches light — the word you would use for a chandelier or a cut glass or anything that is in the business of shining.

He started it when I was about four, in the courtyard of the house in Mirdamad [meer-daa-MAAD], with a screwdriver in his hand. I would come into a room with a face like a closed shop and he would say, in front of whoever was there, ah, here he is. Ali Boloor. The light of the house.

And everybody would laugh, including me, eventually, at about seven, once I had understood the joke — which is that I was the least shining object in that apartment and he had decided to call me the shiniest, every day, for years, until it became the thing I was called.

I want to be very careful about how this is read, because there is a version of a book like this in which the nickname is a cruelty and the childhood is cold and the boy goes south because there is nothing at home.
That is not what happened and I will not have it.

I was loved. Enormously, obviously, and by everybody in that apartment. My mother and my father did not argue. I want that put down exactly, because a reader will hear it as a good thing and it was not one. What they had instead was a silence — a calm, courteous, respectful silence that could settle over a dinner table for the whole of a meal, with the radio on low in the kitchen, and that had a door shut somewhere inside it, about money in the early years and about my grandfather’s firm in the later ones — and I sat inside it the way every child on earth sits inside whatever the weather of his house is, and it never once occurred to me that the house was not solid, because the house was solid.

It was a warm house in every room except the one my parents were both in. There was always somebody in the kitchen. My father came home at seven and asked me what I had done and listened to the answer, and then went into whatever room it was he went into inside his own head, and stayed there until dinner. My mother taught me to look at paintings before I could read, sitting on the floor with a book open on both our knees, and the reason I can walk into a museum in another country now and not feel like a fraud is entirely her.
I was an introvert in a loving house. Those are two separate facts and I spent years letting people assume the second one explained the first.

It did not. I was simply made that way, and my grandfather — who was made the other way — found it funny, and decided the correct response was to call me the light of the house every Friday for five years, and my father, who was made the other way too, laughed every time and never once said it himself.
Nobody has called me Boloor since Aban [aa-BAAN] of 1376.

That is the sentence. My mother could not do it. My father tried once, about a month afterwards, in a doorway, and got one syllable out and stopped. Amir said it exactly once more, four years later, over a plate of watermelon, as an insult, which is the only way it could still be said, and I will get to it.
And that was that. A word that had been said out loud in that family several hundred times simply stopped existing, on a Tuesday, and nobody discussed the decision, because there was no decision.

I did not like being looked at. I did not like being asked what I thought about something at a table. When people came to the apartment I went to my room, and the door of that room was, from about the age of ten, the most important object in my life.
And behind it there was a PlayStation.
I want to put this down properly because a reader outside will not have it and because it is the whole of my adolescence.

The console came from Paytakht [pay-TAKHT], which is a building off Mirdamad full of small computer shops on four floors, and where in 1381 you could buy any game in the world for the price of a sandwich, on a burned disc, in a paper sleeve, with the name written on it in marker in someone’s handwriting.

Nothing was legitimate. Nothing had ever been legitimate. An entire generation of us grew up on pirated everything and never once thought about it, and the discs skipped in the same places, and you learned to hold the console at an angle.
I played, at a conservative estimate, four thousand hours between the ages of ten and fifteen.

And the games I played were the ones with nobody in them. That is the tell, and I did not see it for twenty years. Not the shooting ones. The ones where you build a thing slowly, alone, at night, with the sound low so the apartment does not know you are awake — a city, a stable of cars, a football club run entirely on spreadsheets in which I was the manager and never the player.
At the same age Amir was in the street.
There was one person.

Sina [SEE-naa]. He lived in the building opposite and he was two years older than me and by the time I was twelve he was a head and a half taller and it stayed that way permanently, and I have never in my life had a friend I did not have to look up at.

Sina was not popular either but he was not unpopular in my way. He was simply enormous and quiet and had absolutely no interest in whether he was in a group, which is a completely different thing from wanting to be in one and failing, and it took me years to work out that we were not the same.
We played together four or five evenings a week for six years. In his room, mostly, because his mother did not mind and mine minded in a way she never said out loud.
And here is what I want on the record.
I never told Sina.
Six years. Four or five evenings a week. My only friend on earth. He knew my grandfather was dead and he knew my mother was difficult and he knew what I thought of my brother.

And every Muharram I disappeared for ten days and came back with my back destroyed and told him I had been at my uncle’s, which was true, and he never asked one further question, because he was sixteen and enormous and quiet and it was not in his nature.
I sat in that boy’s room with my shirt stuck to me and played video games with him and did not tell him, and I do not have a single good reason.

The best I have is this: everything about the yard worked because nobody down there knew about the north, and I think somewhere underneath I understood that it would also stop working if anybody in the north knew about the yard.
I had built a wall through the middle of a fifteen-year-old and I was maintaining it in both directions and I thought this was normal.
Amir and I were close until he was about thirteen.
I want that on the record too, because the easy version of this is that my brother was awful to me and he was not, not once, not ever, and that is somehow harder.

When I was six and he was ten he taught me to play chess and lost to me on purpose for about a year before I noticed. When our grandfather died he came into my room and sat on the floor with his back against my bed, every night, for eleven nights, and said nothing, because I was not saying anything, and he had worked out that leaving would be worse.
Eleven nights, on a floor, at thirteen.

And then he turned fourteen and the phone started and the street started, and it was not cruelty, it was simply that the world opened for him at exactly the speed it was closing for me, and he went out into it because that is what you do.
He did not push me away. He drifted, at the ordinary rate, and I let the distance become the point, because by then I had a mechanism for turning things I could not have into things I had chosen.
Red and blue. North and south. Him and me.
By the time I was fifteen we had one real conversation a month and it was about football, and it was hostile, and it was the warmest thing in the house.
There is a thing he said to me in the summer of 1382, months after everything, when my hands were still in dressings and he was home from Tabriz [tab-REEZ].
He looked at my hands for a long time — he had not been told the true thing and never has been — and he said:
You know you could have just been bad at school like a normal person.
And I laughed. It was the first time I had laughed since Esfand [es-FAND].
And then he said, and this is the part, this is the whole of my brother and the reason I brought a photograph eleven thousand kilometres:
He said: Whatever it is you go down there for. Is it working?
Not what is it. Not who are they. Not why.
Is it working.
And I said yes.
And he said: Good.
And went to get his phone.

Seven years later I was in a queue at Imam Khomeini airport at four in the morning and Amir was not there, because he was in Toronto by then and had been for two years, and had gone the way our sort of family goes, which is legally, in a straight line, with documents, with nobody at the airport crying.
I went the other way. Sponsored, lawyered, two and a half years, a man in Vanak [va-NAK] with a photograph of his son in a graduation gown, and a bill that I believed for eleven years I had paid.
Two brothers out of the same eighth-floor apartment in Elahieh.
He is in a house with a mortgage and a garden and a red scarf in a drawer and he has never once had to explain his hands to anybody.
I am the other one.

I have always been the other one. I selected it at seven years old at a table where everybody agreed about something, and I have never in my life been able to work out whether that was the beginning of me or the end.
3. THE NIGHT — the summer of 1381
I am going to stop the funeral for a chapter.

There is a lot of death in this book and a certain amount of blood on concrete and I have been walking you through the worst ten days of my life at the pace of a man who does not want to arrive. Before I go any further I want to put down the best three months I ever had, because they happened, and because a reader who only has the winter of me does not have me.
Khordad [khor-DAAD] 1381. I am thirteen, two months off fourteen. Third year of rahnamayi [rah-na-maa-YEE] — middle school, the last of the three years, the end of it.

And at the end of that year every third-year student in the country sits the same paper, at the same hour, on the same day. It was called the Sarasari [sa-raa-sa-REE], which means nationwide, across-the-whole-thing, and that is exactly what it felt like: a single sheet of paper laid across sixty million people, and every thirteen-year-old in Iran pinned under it at nine in the morning simultaneously.
It decides what school you go on to. Which decides, in the way that these things decide in this country, a very large amount of everything.
I was not a good student. I want that on the record because people assume, from how I turned out and where I ended up, that I must have been.
I was a terrible student who got acceptable results by a method that would horrify any teacher alive.
I did not learn the books. I memorised them.

Physically, out loud, walking. I walked circles round that apartment — kitchen, hall, past my mother’s door, dining room, back to the kitchen — with the book open in one hand at chest height, reading a paragraph, looking away, saying it, looking back, saying it again.
Then the next one. Then both. Then the page. Then the two pages.

Not the concept. Not the reasoning. The words, in order, including the diagram captions, including in one case a printing error that I reproduced faithfully in an exam because I did not know it was an error.

I did four thousand laps of that apartment between the ages of eleven and fourteen. My mother — an art historian, a woman who had taught me to look at a painting for twenty minutes before saying anything about it — used to stand in a doorway and watch me go past reciting the water cycle in a flat voice, and I know now what was on her face and at the time I thought she was checking whether I was working.
The last night. Fourteenth of Khordad, 1381.

Nobody sleeps. That is not a figure of speech and it is not just me — that is a national event. On the night before the Sarasari there are lights on in every apartment block in this city at three in the morning, and if you go out onto a balcony you can see them, floor after floor after floor, and every one of those windows has a thirteen-year-old behind it and a mother making tea.
My mother made tea. She made it four times. She did not ask me anything, which was the correct decision and which I did not appreciate for fifteen years.
At about two Amir came in. He was seventeen and had done this himself four years earlier and had, of course, been fine.
He did not offer to test me. He put a plate of watermelon on the desk, cut properly, cold, and said: Boloor is going to fail and become a taxi driver and I will be embarrassed at parties.
And went out.
And I ate the entire plate at half past two in the morning with a geography book open in front of me and I want to say now that it is one of the four or five happiest memories I have.
I slept about ninety minutes. I sat the paper. It was not as bad as anything I had imagined at three in the morning, which is a thing I have since learned is true of nearly everything.

I came out at half past eleven on the fifteenth of Khordad, 1381, into a street full of thirteen-year-olds, all of whom had finished at the same instant, all over the country, and this is the thing about a nationwide exam that nobody tells you: the summer starts for everyone at exactly the same second.
Sixty million people’s worth of children walking out of buildings into sunlight at half past eleven in the morning simultaneously.
I have never felt anything like it since and I do not expect to.
I went home. I put the books in a bag. I did not open one of them again for eighty-eight days.
And the next morning at nine o’clock I took a taxi to Paytakht.
Paytakht means the capital. That is all it means. The capital city.

And it was a building — four floors of it, off Mirdamad, with a name like a government department and the actual contents of a bazaar. Small units, glass fronts, each one about the size of a shipping container, each one run by a man in his twenties who knew everything.

Consoles behind glass. Controllers hanging on pegboard. And discs — thousands and thousands of discs, in paper sleeves, in racks, in shoeboxes, in stacks on the counter, and every single one of them burned, and every single one of them with the title written on the face in permanent marker in the shopkeeper’s own handwriting.

Nothing in that building was legitimate and it did not occur to anybody that it might be. An entire generation of us learned what a video game was from a disc a man had copied in the back of a shop off Mirdamad for the price of two sandwiches. It was two streets from my grandmother’s house, where my grandfather had sat in the courtyard taking apart things that did not need taking apart, and I went past her gate most mornings that summer and did not go in, and I have no defence for that either.

You could take a disc back if it did not work. There was no receipt and there was no policy. You went back and said it doesn’t run past the second level and he took it and gave you another one, because he was going to see you again in eleven days and both of you knew it.
I went most mornings that summer. Alone, usually.

A taxi from Elahieh down through the top of the city in the early sun. That specific Tehran morning light which is very white and very hard and comes off the walls. The traffic beginning to build but not yet the real thing. The windows down. A driver with the radio on, and every driver in this city has an opinion and shares it.
I was thirteen and had money from Nowruz and no obligations of any kind and I was going to a four-storey building full of games.

I want you to understand: no obligations. None. In this country, in that class, in that year, a boy’s summer between rahnamayi and dabirestan [da-bee-res-TAAN] is the last completely empty container he is ever handed. There was nothing. No school, no tutor, no plan.
Except judo, in the evenings, four days a week, in a hall in Gholhak [ghol-HAK] with a sprung floor and a smell that I could describe for a page.
And Sina.

He came with me perhaps one morning in four, and when he did the entire character of the trip changed, because Sina was by that summer already a hundred and ninety centimetres — six foot three — and I was, at thirteen, extremely not.

We looked ridiculous. I have to say it plainly. There was a full head and a half between us. People turned round. In taxis the driver would look in the mirror at Sina folded into the back seat with his knees against the front and then at me and say something, and it was almost always the same joke in one of its four variations, and Sina had a way of absorbing it that I studied for years and never learned.
A shopkeeper on the third floor of Paytakht called us the exclamation mark for an entire summer.

And I loved it. That is the part I did not expect to be writing at thirty-four. I loved being looked at when I was next to him. I hated being looked at every other second of my life and I have organised my entire existence around not being looked at, and walking through Mirdamad next to an enormous quiet sixteen-year-old while people turned their heads was the only version of it I have ever enjoyed.
Odd, again. Everything about me, odd, again, and for once it did not cost anything.
The days went like this.

Paytakht in the morning. Home by one with two or three discs. Something to eat that my mother had left. Then the room, the door shut, the curtains half across because of the glare, and the machine on.
Six hours. Seven. The apartment enormous and quiet and hot, the sound of the city coming up eight floors and arriving softened, a fan going.
Judo at six. Come back at eight destroyed and pleased.
And then, two or three nights a week, Sina slept over.
Those nights are the best thing I own.

We played until three, until four, until it started to get light, on a fourteen-inch television on the floor with our backs against my bed, and there was a specific hour — around half past three — when the whole city genuinely went quiet, and you would hear one motorbike four streets away, and that was all.
And the thing I liked best in the entire world was this, and it is going to sound strange:
I liked watching him play the frightening ones.
I did not play them. I could not. I would get four minutes into one of those games and have to put the controller down and pretend I needed water.
So Sina played and I watched.

He would take the controller and go into whatever hospital or town or house it was, and he was completely fearless in a way that I now think was mostly just a very slow nervous system, and I sat next to him on the floor at two in the morning with a cushion in my lap and watched.

And when it happened — whatever it was, the thing behind the door, the thing in the corridor — Sina would say a single quiet word and keep walking forward, and I would have my whole face in the cushion, and we would both be laughing so hard we had to pause it in case my mother woke up.

That was it. That is the whole activity. A boy of thirteen watching a boy of sixteen walk down a corridor in a haunted building on a fourteen-inch television at two in the morning in Elahieh in the summer of 1381.
I have had a certain number of good hours in my life. Those are the best ones and it is not close.
Eighty-eight days.

Mirdamad in the sun. Watermelon at two in the morning. A sprung floor in Gholhak. My mother in a doorway not asking me anything. My brother insulting me tenderly and leaving. An enormous friend folded into the back of a taxi.
And underneath all of it, so quiet that summer that I genuinely did not think about it for weeks at a time:
Muharram was in Esfand.

It was eight months away. It had been going on for four years by then and it was the fixed spine of my life and I did not think about it once between Khordad and Shahrivar [shah-ree-VAR] of 1381, because I was thirteen and it was summer and I was happy.
That is what I want on the record before the rest of this book happens.

I was not a haunted child. I was not a lonely child in any way that a doctor would write down. I had a mother who loved me and a father who asked me every evening what I had done and a brother who put watermelon on my desk and a friend the size of a door and a room with a machine in it and three months of sunlight with nothing in them at all.
And then Esfand came, the way it comes every year, and I got on the number 130 and went south.
Nobody made me.
That is the part I have never been able to explain to anybody in America.
Nobody ever once made me.
4. THE NIGHT — what a heyat actually is

Before any of it goes wrong, I want to explain what one of these things is, in the plain way nobody ever bothers to, because a reader outside this country has been given two pictures and both of them are wrong.
The first wrong picture is the news picture: a mob, blood, fanaticism, a wall of shouting men.
The second wrong picture is the tourist one: an ancient and beautiful folk tradition, colourful, photographed at golden hour, with a caption about the mystical East.

Neither of those is a heyat [hey-AT]. A heyat is closer to a working men’s club that has a religion attached to it, and it is one of the most quietly functional institutions I have ever encountered anywhere in the world, and I have now lived in another country and I have not seen its equal.
Ours had about three hundred and forty regular men and had existed, in one form or another, since about 1327 — 1948 — when it was five men in a basement on a street that is not there any more.

It had a treasurer. That is the first unglamorous fact. There was a ledger, and it was inspected, badly, once a year by three men who did not like each other, which is the correct number of men and the correct relationship between them.

It owned things. A steel trunk of chains. Two dohols. Three cauldrons and the gas burners for them. Eleven metres of tarpaulin. A generator. A PA system that was better than the PA system of the local school. Four hundred metres of black cloth with the verses printed on it, folded in sacks that said SAMAN RICE. And an alam [a-LAM], which was brass and had been paid for in 1341 by eleven men putting in a month’s wages each, and whose names were on a piece of paper inside the storeroom door that nobody read and nobody threw away.
And it did things. This is what nobody tells you.

It buried people. If you died in that quarter and you were of that heyat, the washing, the shroud, the plot, the transport, the three days of food for your family and the hall for the seventh and the fortieth were handled, and nobody sent your widow a bill, and nobody discussed the money in front of her, ever.

It lent money. Interest-free, informally, from a fund that was not written in the ledger and that everybody knew about. A man needed a deposit on a shop, or his daughter was getting married, or the hospital wanted a number he did not have. He went to Nemat. It was never called a loan and it was always repaid.
It found people work. About a third of the men in that yard had at some point been employed by another man in that yard.
It went to prisons. Two of the older men did that and nobody talked about it.
And once a year it fed four hundred families for two days.
Now. I am going to say the uncomfortable thing, because this book is not a defence.
Every single one of those functions is a function that a state performs in a country where the state performs functions.
Burial, welfare, small credit, employment, care of prisoners, food relief. That is a municipality. That is what a municipality is.
And in the south of this city, in my lifetime, a large amount of it was done instead by several hundred volunteer associations organised around the commemoration of a death in Iraq in the year 680.
That is not mysticism. That is infrastructure with a story bolted to the front of it.

And the story is load-bearing. That is the part that matters and that took me until my late twenties to see. You could not run that system on civic feeling. You could not run it on charity, because charity has a giver and a receiver and men in that quarter would rather go hungry than be seen receiving. You certainly could not run it on the state, which had other priorities.
But you can run it on a vow.

Because a vow has no giver and no receiver. A vow is a debt to God that happens to be settled in your neighbour’s direction, and a man taking a bowl of nazri [naz-REE] out of my hands on Ashura [aa-shoo-RAA] is not accepting charity from me, he is helping me pay something I owe. He is doing me the favour.
That is a thirteen-hundred-year-old piece of social engineering and it is the most elegant thing I have ever seen a religion do, and it is why I cannot write the easy version of this book.
And.

The same machine that buries your father and pays your hospital bill without ever saying the word money is the machine that decides where a boy stands, and how heavy his chain is, and at what speed the drum goes, and what he is told when he asks a question, and whether a death in a yard behind a green gate becomes a fact or becomes the word Dubai.

It is one machine. You do not get the burial without the arrangement. There is no version of that yard that feeds four hundred families and also tells a fifteen-year-old the truth on the seventh night, because the same instinct does both — close around it, hold it, keep the day coming, do not let anyone fall out of the row.
Everything good about that place and everything that happened to me came out of the same organ.

I have been in rooms in America where people were free and honest and nobody had lied to me about anything, and when my grandfather Yousef died there was nobody at the door with food, and I stood in a kitchen and thought about a yard with three cauldrons in it, and I want to be extremely clear that I did not, in that moment, think I had got the better end of the deal.
PART TWO — THE BANNERS
5. THE NIGHT — Nazi Abad, the first of Muharram
The banners go up before the month does. That is the first thing to understand about my street. We are early. We are early the way people are early to a funeral when they are afraid of the family.

Agha Rahmat brings out the ladder on the twenty-eighth of Zilhajjeh, which is two days before anything is supposed to start, and he leans it against the shutter of his own shop, and nobody stops him, because who is going to stop a man from hanging black cloth. His son holds the base. The cloth comes out of a plastic sack that says SAMAN RICE on it in green, and it comes out folded, and it smells like the sack and like last year.

I watch from the step of my uncle’s building with my hands inside my sleeves. It is Esfand, which is our deep winter, and the cold in Tehran that month is not a soft cold. It is a cold with an opinion. You can see the Alborz [al-BORZ] from the top of our street if you stand in the right place and the air is having a good day, and the mountains are white all the way down to where the city starts, and the city is the colour of a dirty coin.

The cloth goes up. Rahmat gets one corner on the hook and then the wind takes the other corner and he stands on the ladder holding one arm of it like he is dancing with a woman much taller than himself.
His son says, Baba, you’re going to fall.
Rahmat says, then catch me.
That is the whole month, actually. Somebody up high, somebody below, an arrangement about catching.

By evening there is black on both sides of the street from the intersection down to the passage. White writing on the black. Every day is Ashura and every land is Karbala [kar-ba-LAA]. You see that sentence so many times in your life here that you stop reading it, the way you stop reading a stop sign, you just obey it. But it is a strange sentence when you actually pick it up and turn it over. It says the thing that happened is not finished. It says it is happening now, on this street, at this bus stop, behind this bakery. It says you are already standing in the desert and just haven’t noticed.
I am fifteen. I have noticed.
Here is what I know at the start of that month, which turned out to be a very small amount, arranged very neatly, like the contents of a wallet belonging to a man who is about to lose it.
I know that we mourn for a man named Hossein [ho-SEYN], who was the grandson of the Prophet, and who was killed in the desert with his family a very long time ago.
I know it was a thousand years ago. This is what everybody says. A thousand years. Later somebody will tell me the real number and it will be worse.
I know that the story has a river in it and that nobody in the story gets to drink from it.
I know that on the tenth night, if I do it correctly, if I do everything correctly, I come out of my body.

I have never told anybody that last one. Not because it’s a secret. Because I assume it is like sweating. I assume it is simply what happens to a person who mourns properly, and that mentioning it would be like announcing to a room that you have kidneys.

Dayi Mehran comes down at eight with his coat already on. Dayi means mother’s brother. I have lived with him for ten days a year for six years and I have never once called him anything else, not his name, nothing, just the word for the relation, which I suppose tells you something about both of us.

He stands in the doorway and does the thing he does before stairs, which is a kind of gathering. He fills up what he can fill. His lungs took mustard gas at a place called Majnoon in a year I wasn’t alive for, and what he has now is about a third of a set of lungs and a very complete set of memories about the other two thirds. He breathes like a man drinking through a straw that has gone flat.
He says, they’ve started already.
I say, Rahmat started already.
He says, Rahmat always starts already. Rahmat would hang black in Farvardin if his wife let him.

And then he laughs and the laugh turns into the other thing, and I look at the wall until it is finished, because that is the arrangement, and he holds the door frame, and when it’s done he says, right, and we go.
6. THE PLAIN — Medina, the year 680
A man in Damascus died, and his son wanted the world to say yes to him.

That is the whole beginning. It is not complicated and people make it complicated. Mo’aviyeh [mo-aa-vee-YEH] died and his son Yazid [ya-ZEED] took the seat, and taking the seat was not enough, because a seat is only a seat. What he wanted was the bay’at [bey-AT] — the pledge. In that time a pledge was a physical act. You put your hand into the hand of the man you were pledging to, and the hand was the contract, because paper can be burned and a hand in a hand is witnessed by everyone standing there.
Yazid wrote to his governor in Medina [me-DEE-na]. The letter was short. Get the pledge from Hossein son of Ali. Do not accept anything else.

Hossein was fifty-six years old. He had grown up in the house of the Prophet, who was his grandfather, and he had been a small child in that house, and the old men of Medina could still remember him being carried on the Prophet’s shoulders in the street. That detail matters. It is not sentiment. It means that everybody in Medina knew exactly whose grandson was being asked to put his hand into that particular hand.

They came for him at night. The governor’s men. Hossein went, and he took thirty of his relatives with him, armed, and left them at the door — which is a way of answering a question before it is asked.
Inside, the governor read the letter aloud.
Hossein said he would not give the pledge in the dark. He said a pledge is a public thing, and if you want it, ask me in the morning, in front of the people.
There was no morning. He left the same night.

He took his family. Not an army — his family. His sons, his brothers, his sister Zaynab [ZEY-nab], his nephews, the women, the children, and a small number of men who had decided a long time ago what they were and were now simply doing it.
They went to Mecca, and they stayed there some months, and while they were there the letters started coming from Kufa [KOO-feh].

Kufa was a city in Iraq that had loved his father. The letters said: come. The letters said: we have no leader and we are waiting. The letters said: the fields are green and the fruit is ripe, come and command us.
There were, by the counting of the old historians, something on the order of twelve thousand of these letters. Sacks of them. Men rode for weeks to deliver them.
Hossein sent his cousin Moslem [MOS-lem] ahead to see whether the letters were true.
They were true when Moslem arrived. Eighteen thousand men put their hands in his hand.

Then Yazid changed the governor of Kufa, and the new governor was a man named Ebn-e Ziad [eb-ne zee-YAAD], and Ebn-e Ziad understood something about crowds that Moslem did not, which is that a crowd is not a number of people, it is a number of people who can see each other. He sent soldiers into the streets at dusk. He told the tribal chiefs that the army of Syria was coming. He arranged for a man to weep publicly and go home.
By nightfall Moslem was standing alone in an alley in a city of eighteen thousand allies, knocking on doors.
One woman let him in. He was found the next day and taken to the roof of the palace and killed and thrown down into the square.

The letter warning Hossein not to come never reached him. He was already on the road with the women and the children and the tents, riding toward a city that had, in the space of a single evening, stopped existing in the form he was riding toward.
7. THE NIGHT — four years earlier
I was eleven the first time I understood what Sohrab [soh-RAAB] Ayeneh [aa-yee-NEH] actually was, and I understood it by accident, from the wrong side of a wall.
Ayeneh means mirror. It is a real family name and there are a few hundred of them in this country and I have never once been able to hear it as an ordinary word.

That year the yard behind the shop was being re-concreted, so for four nights the heyat met in the hall of the boys’ school two streets over, which had a stage and a curtain and a smell of feet, and which was the wrong building for it in every conceivable way.
I was eleven and I was small and I had the job that small boys have, which is the tea.

You carry a tray of glasses through a standing crowd of grown men in the dark. That is the job. Nobody teaches you and there is no technique except that you hold the tray at the height of your own chin and you go where the gaps are and men move for you without looking, and by the end of it your forearms are shaking and you have been scalded twice and you would not trade the job for anything on earth, because for two hours you are the only person in the building who is allowed to move.
So I saw it from underneath. I want that noted. Everything I know about how a room like that works, I learned at the height of a tray.
There is a thing a maddah [mad-DAAH] does at the beginning that nobody notices, and I only noticed it because I was standing in the wrong place.
He walks in early. Twenty minutes early, before it fills, when there are thirty men in a room built for four hundred. And he does not go to the microphone. He walks the room.

Sohrab did a circuit of that school hall like a man checking a car he was thinking of buying. He put his hand flat on a wall. He walked into the middle and clapped once — one clap, and stood still, and listened to it come back off the ceiling. He went to the back corner and clapped again.
Then he went and said something to the man on the mixer and the man on the mixer changed something, and Sohrab clapped once more, and nodded, and that was that.
I asked him about it years later, when I was fourteen and had become a person he would answer.
He said: every room lies to you differently.

He said: in this yard the wall behind you sends it back at you a quarter-beat late, so if you are not careful you start chasing your own voice and you speed up all night and by the end you are running and nobody can breathe. In the school hall it went up into the ceiling and died, so you had to push, and if you push for two hours you have nothing left on the tenth.
He said: they think I am singing. I am doing arithmetic.

He was twenty-one that year. He was very good-looking in a way that men in that neighbourhood dealt with by making jokes about it, and he had a small motorbike he was ashamed of, and he had a job at a printer’s in Molavi [mo-la-VEE] where he set type and came home with ink in the creases of his hands.
And he was, I have to say this plainly, kind to children in a way that adults usually are not — which is that he was kind to us when nobody was watching, which is the only kind that counts.
Here is the thing he did for me and it took him four seconds.

I came through the crowd with the tray and got jammed. Genuinely jammed, wedged between two men’s backs, tray at chin height, arms gone, eleven years old, about to drop nine glasses of boiling tea on a carpet in front of the entire street.

And Sohrab, who was on the microphone, who was three minutes from starting, who had four hundred men waiting on him — put his hand over the head of it and said, into the room, in a completely ordinary voice:
Agha, move for the tea.
And two hundred men turned round and made a corridor.

He did not look at me while I went down it. That is the part. He looked at his paper. He gave me a road and then declined to watch me use it, which at eleven I did not have words for and which I now understand was the entire man.
That night was the first time I ever heard him do the thing with the low note.

He gets to the top of the nowheh [now-HEH] — the lament, the sung part, the one the crowd answers — and there is a place where the melody wants to go up. Everybody in the room knows it wants to go up. Everybody in the room is leaning.
And he sat on the note underneath it.
Once. Twice. A third time. Four hundred men leaning forward like a field of wheat under a wind, and this man in a black shirt at a microphone in a school hall refusing, and refusing, and refusing.

And then, when he finally gave it, the sound the room made was not a cheer and it was not weeping, it was something between, and I was eleven and standing under a tray and the hair came up on my arms.

I did not go out of my body that night. It was the fourth night and I was eleven and it had already happened to me twice, the first time on the eighth night and the second on the tenth, both times at the front.
But I remember thinking, with a tray in my hands, in a school hall that smelled of feet:
He is doing it to them. Whatever happens to me, he is the one doing it.
I was closer than I knew and I was completely wrong about the direction.
He carried the alam in the shabih [sha-BEEH] that year. He carried it six years in total and I saw five of them.
And I want to put down what it looked like, because I am the last person alive who is going to.

He walked it slower than anyone. That was all. There is no trick in it. The scene is four metres of carpet and a strip of blue cloth held by two boys and a waterskin, and every other man who has ever done it walks it in about nine seconds.
Sohrab took twenty-two. I counted, the last year, because by then I was fourteen and had started counting things.
Twenty-two seconds to cross four metres of carpet, in a yard with four hundred men in it, in total silence, holding a brass hand on a pole.
And when he knelt and filled the skin and lifted the water to his mouth, he held it there.
He held water in his cupped hands in front of four hundred people for — and I know this because I counted that too — nine seconds.
Nine seconds is an extremely long time. Try it. Put your hands up in front of your face and count to nine and imagine four hundred men not breathing.
Then he put it back.
Four years later I was given his part and nobody told me it had been his, and I walked it in about eleven seconds, and I thought I was magnificent.
And a year before that, in a yard behind a green gate, at four in the morning, eleven men who loved him stood around him for eleven minutes and discussed it.
He was twenty-four.
He could hear a room. He was the only person I have ever met who could hear a room.
8. THE PLAIN — the road, and the man who turned them
They went north from Mecca in a caravan you could have counted from a rooftop.
Somewhere on that road a rider came the other way and told Hossein about Moslem. About the roof, and the square.

He stopped the caravan. He gathered everyone who was travelling with him — including a number of men who had joined along the way believing they were riding toward a city of eighteen thousand friends and a green season — and he told them the truth, out loud, in front of the women and the animals.
Then he said: whoever wants to go, go. There is no obligation on you. Take the night.

Most of them went. This is written down and it is not hidden and I think it should be said more often than it is. The caravan that left Mecca was substantially larger than the caravan that continued the next morning. People did the arithmetic and the arithmetic was not difficult.
What was left was mostly family, and a small number who were not family and stayed anyway.
In the last week of the journey they met the cavalry.

A thousand horsemen under a commander named Hurr [HORR]. They came out of the heat and they came fast and they positioned themselves across the road, and the first thing anyone noticed was that the horses were finished — heads down, sides going like bellows — and the men on them were grey in the face.
They had been riding since before dawn without water.
Hossein looked at them and said: water the horsemen. And water the horses.

His people got up and did it. They poured for a thousand men and however many animals, and where a man was too far gone to hold the bowl they tilted it for him, and they went on pouring until the caravan’s own water was measurably lower.

Hurr’s orders were to cut Hossein off from the road and not let him turn back and not let him go forward, and to keep him in open country until further instruction. He had come to arrest a man and the man had watered him.

He rode alongside them after that. Not with them. Alongside. For days. He prayed behind Hossein and he blocked his road in the same afternoon, and if you want to know what that is like, it is like every one of us on this street, all month, every year.
They pushed them off the road and out into flat ground near the river, near a place with a small name. Hossein asked what the place was called.
They gave him a few names. Then somebody said the local people call it Karbala.
He is reported to have repeated it. Karb and bala. Grief and affliction.
He said, here. Put down the tents here.

That was the second day of Muharram, and there were eight days left, and they had six hundred metres of open ground between the tents and the river, and for five of those days nobody stopped them from walking down to it whenever they were thirsty.
9. THE NIGHT — the second night, and the part
Our heyat is called Heyat-e Bani Fatemeh [BA-nee faa-te-MEH] and it meets in the yard behind Haj Nemat’s shop.

Heyat is one of those words that everyone uses and nobody explains. It’s Arabic. It means a body, a shape, a form — a group of people that has taken a shape. And that’s exactly right, because a heyat is a street’s grief that has been organised until it has a shape, and once it has a shape it also has a treasurer and a storage cupboard and an argument about who gets to hold the standard.

Haj Nemat is a butcher. His shop faces the main road and the yard is behind it, walled, with a steel gate that is always closed and never locked, which is a distinction I did not think about at all until later.

In the yard there is a tarpaulin strung between the wall and the back of the shop, and under the tarpaulin there are carpets laid edge to edge, and they are good carpets that have been ruined in a specific way, worn flat in strips where men kneel. There are bulbs on a cable. There is a generator that they only start when the power goes, and the power goes.

And there are the cauldrons. Three of them, and they are not pots, they are architecture. The big one comes up past my hip. You could bathe a child in it. It’s called a deeg [DEEG] and it lives on its side against the wall for eleven months of the year with a piece of plastic over it like a horse under a blanket.
On the second night the yard is half full and the fluorescent tube over the door is doing the thing where it can’t decide.

Haj Nemat comes out with a glass of tea and does not drink it. He is fifty-something and built like a door and he has forearms from thirty years of the work. He stands next to me and looks at the yard the way I imagine a captain looks at weather.
He says, Ali jan. This year you’re Abbas.
I do not say anything for a second because there is nothing in my mouth.

You have to understand what he has just handed me. Every year on the ninth night the heyat does a shabih — a resemblance. That is the older word for it, and it’s a better word than the polite one. The polite word is ta’ziyeh [ta-zee-YEH], from the Arabic for condolence, and it makes it sound like a play. Shabih-khani means resemblance-reading. It does not mean you act as somebody. It means you resemble him, and for a few minutes the resemblance is the closest thing available.
And Abbas is the part. Abbas is Hossein’s brother. Abbas is the one who carried the standard. Abbas is the one who went to the river.
I say, me?
He says, you’re tall enough now.
I say, but who —

And he turns and walks back into the shop, and the sentence I was going to finish was but who had it before, and I have thought about that unfinished sentence probably four thousand times since, and I want to be very clear that he did not dodge it. He simply left before it arrived. There is a difference. I have had nineteen years to decide whether there is a difference and I have decided there is, and I am not sure I believe myself.
Dayi Mehran is sitting on a plastic chair at the back with the old men. He is thirty-six and he sits with the old men because of the chairs.
I go and tell him.
He says, Abbas.
I say, Abbas.
He looks at me for a while. He has a way of looking at you where you can hear him breathing and it becomes part of the looking.
Then he says, do you know what Abbas actually did?
He got the water.
He says, no. Anyone can get water. Do you know what he did?

And I don’t, not properly, not then, and he can see that I don’t, and he does something that at the time I found irritating and that I now understand was the single kindest thing anyone did for me that entire month.
He says: I’m not telling you. Go and listen.
10. THE PLAIN — Kufa, the night of the eighteen thousand
I have to go backwards for this one, to before Karbala, to the part of the story that explains everything that happens afterwards, and which most people skip because there is no battle in it.
You will remember that Hossein was in Mecca, and that the letters started coming from Kufa.

Kufa was not a village. Kufa was one of the great cities of the world at that moment — a garrison town in Iraq that had grown into a capital, tens of thousands of people, and it had been the seat of Hossein’s father Ali when he ruled. Kufa had loved that family within living memory. Old men in Kufa had prayed behind Ali. The city considered itself, and said so in writing, the natural home of his line.
And when Mo’aviyeh died in Damascus and his son Yazid took the seat, Kufa wrote.
The letters are not a legend. The number given in the old histories is around twelve thousand and even if you cut it by nine tenths it is an extraordinary thing.

They came in sacks. Riders carried them across the desert in relays. Some were from tribal chiefs and some were from ordinary men and some carried a hundred signatures because a hundred men had put their names on one sheet in a courtyard.
And what they said, over and over, in different hands, was: we have no leader. Come. The fields are green and the fruit is ripe and we are waiting for you.
Imagine receiving that. Imagine sitting in Mecca with a sack of twelve thousand pieces of paper in front of you, each one a man saying I am with you.
Hossein did not simply believe it. That is important. He sent someone to check.

He sent Moslem ibn Aqil [MOS-lem eb-ne a-GHEEL]. His cousin. His father’s brother’s son, so a man of the household, trusted absolutely, and — this is the detail that gets me — Moslem took two of his own young sons with him, which is what a man does when he does not think he is going to a war.
Moslem got to Kufa and the city opened.
He stayed in the house of a leading man of the city and men came to him in a steady stream for days, and each of them put his hand into Moslem’s hand and gave the pledge.
Eighteen thousand.
Moslem wrote to Hossein in Mecca and the letter said, in effect: it is true. Come. Eighteen thousand men have given the pledge to me in your name.
And on the strength of that letter, Hossein put his sister and his sons and his daughters and his infant on camels and started for Iraq.
Now. What happened next took one evening, and it is the most instructive evening in the whole of human history, and it is not about Iraq in the year 680.
Yazid replaced the governor. The new man was Ebn-e Ziad, and he arrived in Kufa at night, alone, with a small party, his face covered.
And the people of Kufa, waiting for Hossein, seeing a covered rider come in at night, came out into the street and cheered him, because they thought he was Hossein.
He let them. He rode through it and let them cheer, all the way to the governor’s palace, and then he went inside and shut the door and in the morning he was the government.
He did four things, and I list them because they are the whole toolkit and they have not changed in thirteen hundred years.
One. He offered a reward for information and a punishment for concealment, and made both of them specific, so that every man in the city knew exactly what his neighbour stood to gain.
Two. He arrested somebody early and did it publicly, so there was a demonstration.

Three. He summoned the tribal chiefs — the men whose names were on the sheets with a hundred signatures under them — and did not threaten them. He talked to them about the army of Syria. He said the word Syria in a room, pleasantly, several times, and let each of them do his own arithmetic about his own sons.
Four. He sent those same chiefs back out into the streets to talk to their own people.

That is the whole method. He did not have soldiers enough to hold Kufa against eighteen thousand men. He never needed them. He simply arranged the city so that no man in it could be certain of the man standing next to him.
Moslem knew it was coming and moved first. He called out the pledge.

And they came. Understand that. It worked. Four thousand men, some accounts say more, assembled in arms and marched on the governor’s palace, and Ebn-e Ziad shut himself inside with a few dozen men, and for about an hour that evening the thing was genuinely, actually won.
Then the chiefs went into the crowd.

They did not fight it. They walked through it talking. A man would find his own uncle beside him saying, quietly, your mother is at home alone. Another would hear that the Syrians were two days out. Another would be told that his brother had already gone.

There is a line in one of the old accounts that I have never got out of my head. It says that a woman came out and took her son by the hand and led him away, and a man came and told his brother it was over, and they went by twos and threes.
By ones and twos and threes. Not a rout. No panic. Nobody ran.
The crowd of four thousand men that had the governor of Iraq trapped in his own palace simply, over about ninety minutes, went home.
And at the end of it Moslem ibn Aqil turned round to give an order and there was nobody behind him.
He walked out of that square alone in the dark.
He walked through the streets of a city where eighteen thousand men had put their hands in his hand inside the previous fortnight, and he knocked on doors.
And the doors did not open.
One did.
A woman named Tow’eh [tow-EH]. She was standing in her own doorway waiting for her son to come home, and a man came out of the dark and asked her for water.

She gave him water. Then he asked to sit down. And she looked at him properly and asked who he was and he told her the truth, which he did not have to do, and she took him in and hid him in a room in her house.
Her son came home. She told him. She made him swear.
He informed the next morning.
They came for Moslem at dawn and he fought them in a doorway and he was wounded and taken up to the roof of the palace, and Ebn-e Ziad had him killed there and his body thrown down into the square.
His two boys were caught later.

And the letter he had sent — come, it is true, eighteen thousand — was already three weeks up the road with a rider, and could not be recalled, and reached nobody, because by then Hossein was already on the desert road with the tents and the women and the infant, riding toward a city that had ceased to exist in the form he was riding toward, and there was no way on earth to tell him.
That is what I mean about this month.

We are not mourning a battle. A battle would be simple. On the tenth day, seventy-two people are killed in an afternoon by an army — but the army is not the point, the army is just what arrives at the end.
The thing that killed them was an evening in a city eighty kilometres away, when eighteen thousand men who meant every word of it went home by twos and threes because somebody spoke to them quietly.
And every single one of those men had signed his name.

That is why the story does not close. That is why we do this every year and will do it next year. Not because a tyrant killed a good man — that happens constantly, that is Tuesday, you do not need a religion for that.
Because eighteen thousand people said I am with you, in writing, and then it got dark.
11. THE NIGHT — the third night, and the going out
I should describe how a night works, because a night has a shape and the shape is the point.

It starts with a man talking. Usually a cleric, sometimes just a serious man with a good voice, and he stands with the microphone and talks about something ordinary — debt, or lying, or how to treat your mother — and it is boring, and it is supposed to be boring. It is the flat ground you stand on before the ground tilts.
Then comes the rowzeh [row-ZEH].

Rowzeh means garden. That’s all. Five hundred years ago a man in Herat wrote a book about the killing at Karbala and he called it The Garden of the Martyrs, and the book was so widely read that after a while people stopped saying “come and hear the reading of the Garden of the Martyrs” and just said “come and hear the Garden,” and then just “the Garden,” and now the word for a garden is the word for the story of a massacre, and nobody notices, and I did not notice until I was fifteen and someone said it slowly.

The man who reads it is the rowzeh-khan [row-zeh-KHAAN]. He tells it as a story, in prose, at a walking pace. He does not sing. He builds. He will take one small hour of one day at Karbala and he will stay inside it for twenty minutes and make you stand there in it, and the whole craft is knowing exactly when to stop building.
And when the room breaks — when the first man goes — he stops.
Then the nowheh starts, and everything changes.

Nowheh is Arabic and it comes from the sound a dove makes. It’s the lament, and it is sung, and it has a beat, and the crowd sings back. There is a lead voice, the maddah, and there is a second man behind him, the zakir [zaa-KER], and zakir means the one who mentions, the one who does not let a name fall out of the world. The zakir has one job. He says Hossein into a microphone, over and over, into a delay unit, so that the name comes back doubled and stacked, and that is not decoration, that is the metronome. The whole street is running on a dead man’s name used as a click track.

The first section is slow. Latmiyeh, from the Arabic for a blow. Open hand on the chest, once a second or slower, three hundred men, and the sound of it is not what you think. It’s wet. It’s a single wet slap that arrives from every direction at once and you feel it in the plate of your own sternum before you have decided to join in.
And then the maddah lifts, and the beat doubles, and that is the shoor [SHOOR].
Shoor is a Persian word that means fervour, ardour, boiling over. It also means salty. Nobody thinks about that. I think about that constantly now.

The third night I am at the front because Haj Nemat has put me at the front, and I do not think anything of this, because I have been at the front since I was nine and by fifteen you no longer ask why the furniture is where it is.

Sohrab’s voice comes out of the speakers. He is not there. He has not been there since last Muharram, because he went to Dubai to work, which is a thing men do, and the heyat plays his recordings because his recordings are the best recordings anyone has. Everyone from three streets over comes to our yard specifically to hear a CD.

I have heard people say his voice was beautiful and that is true but it undersells it. What Sohrab could do was withhold. He could sit on the low note and refuse to give you the high one, four times, five times, until the yard was leaning forward like a field of wheat, and then he would still not give it, and then he would.
The shoor comes in. Four hundred and something men on the beat. The bulbs on the cable are swinging because someone has knocked the wall.
And I go.
I want to say this carefully because everyone gets it wrong when they imagine it.
It is not a bang. Nothing tears. There is no tunnel and there is no light and nobody is waiting.

What happens is that the effort stops. That’s all. For six hours you have been holding something up — your name, your face, the fact of being a specific boy from a specific street with a specific dead grandfather and a specific silent father — and it is so heavy that you never notice you’re holding it, because you have held it since birth and have nothing to compare it to. And then, on a particular beat, at a particular volume, you put it down.
And the relief is so enormous that the first year it happened I cried for an hour afterwards and could not tell anybody why.

The boy below is in the third row from the tarpaulin, and his hands are moving on the beat without him. From up here the crowd is not men. It is one animal breathing. The bulbs are yellow and swinging and the tarpaulin has a tear in the corner that nobody has fixed in nine years. Haj Nemat is standing by the shop door with his arms folded and he is not beating his chest and he is not weeping and he is not looking at the crowd.
He is looking at the boy.

I come back somewhere in the last ten minutes. There is no seam. You are simply in your body again and your throat is destroyed and your chest is hot and the man beside you is holding you up by the elbow the way men do, without comment, and you hold the next one up, and that is the arrangement.
Walking home Dayi Mehran doesn’t talk, because the cold air is a bad customer for him.
At the door he says: good night?
I say: good night.

I have said this exact thing to him for six years and he has said his exact thing back, and neither of us knows what the other one means by it, and I would give a great deal to have that conversation again now that I do.
12. THE PLAIN — the second to the sixth of Muharram
For five days almost nothing happened, and this is the part that gets left out, and it should not be, because it is the part that makes the rest unbearable.

They camped. Seventy-two men, and the women, and the children, and the tents in a curve with the family in the middle. They had the river. Six hundred metres of flat ground and then the Euphrates, and anyone could walk down and fill a skin whenever they liked. Children went down to it. People washed.

On the third day the army arrived from Kufa, four thousand under a commander named Omar son of Sa’d, and over the following days more came, and the number kept climbing until nobody bothered counting precisely. The old books say the final figure was somewhere in the tens of thousands. Even taking the lowest honest estimate you have several thousand professional soldiers arranged in a crescent against seventy-two men, most of whom were related to each other.
And then they negotiated. For days.

Omar son of Sa’d did not want to do this. That is documented and it is the most modern thing in the entire story. He was not a monster. He was an ordinary competent officer who had been offered the governorship of Rey [RAY] — which is here, which is a district of this city, which is about forty minutes from that yard — as payment for this specific job. He wrote to Ebn-e Ziad in Kufa proposing settlements. Let him go back. Let him go to a frontier. Let him go anywhere.
Ebn-e Ziad wrote back one line: get the pledge or cut him off from the water.
And Omar son of Sa’d read that, and thought about Rey, and gave the order.
That is what a man is. Not the men with the swords. The man with the letter in his hand doing arithmetic about a district of Tehran.
13. THE NIGHT — the fifth night, the chains
The chains come out on the fifth.

They live in a steel trunk in Haj Nemat’s storeroom under a piece of felt, and they are counted out into your hand by an old man called Agha Sadegh who has done this job for so long that nobody remembers deciding he had it.

A zanjeer [zan-JEER] is a wooden or plastic grip, palm-sized, and hanging off it a cluster of flat blunt chain links, twenty or thirty of them, each about the length of your finger. Blunt. It is important that you understand they are blunt, and it is important that you understand what several hundred grams of blunt metal thrown at speed will do to skin over four hours.

You throw it over the right shoulder. Then the left. On the beat. Right, left, right, left, and the men are in rows of twenty and the rows are locked and if you break the rhythm you hit the man beside you, so you do not break the rhythm, and that fact — that your neighbour’s back depends on your timing — is doing more work in that yard than any theology.
The first hour is loud and stupid and almost fun.
The second hour your shoulders find the place where the links land and the place becomes a single hot stripe rather than a set of individual hits.
The third hour the stripe stops being pain and becomes information. It’s just data. My back is doing something. The report is filed and nobody reads it.
Somewhere in the fourth hour you notice you can no longer feel the difference between your body and the sound.
Agha Sadegh counts them out and when he gets to me he does the thing he always does, which is take one back.
He puts a zanjeer in my hand and then holds his palm out and I give it back and he gives me a different one from the bottom of the trunk. Every year. Since I was nine.

I said something about it once, when I was eleven, something like why do I get that one, and he said because that one’s yours, and I accepted this completely, because when you are eleven and a man tells you a specific object is yours that is the most satisfying sentence in the language.

Mine is lighter. Not obviously. Not so you’d stare. Two-thirds the weight, maybe. Fewer links and thinner ones and a grip worn smooth by somebody else’s hand for years before it was worn smooth by mine.

I found that out at thirty-three, eleven thousand kilometres away, when I lifted somebody else’s out of a plastic crate in a rented hall in Los Angeles and nearly put myself on the floor with it, and put it straight back.
But that is the second book and I am getting ahead.

That fifth night I bleed for the first time, properly, not a graze — an actual line of it running down inside the back of my shirt, warm and then instantly cold in the Esfand air, and I put my hand back there at the break and look at my fingers under the bulb.

And what I feel is relief. Enormous, embarrassing relief. Because it means I’ve done it right. It means I’m in. Nobody in that yard would say that out loud, and every single man in it knows exactly what I mean.
Mehran sees me looking at my hand.
He says, show me.
I turn around and he lifts the shirt and looks and puts it down and says nothing at all, and starts breathing badly, and I assume it is the cold.
14. THE PLAIN — the seventh of Muharram
On the seventh the order was carried out.

Five hundred cavalry were positioned between the tents and the Euphrates. Not to fight. To stand there. That is all it took. Six hundred metres of open ground and five hundred horses on it, and from that afternoon the camp had whatever was already in its skins and nothing else, and it was Iraq, and it was the beginning of October by our reckoning, and there were fifty-odd children in those tents.

The soldiers did not shout at them. Understand that. There was no cruelty in it that would look like cruelty in a photograph.
