They stood in the sun by the water and they filled their own skins from it, and men who had known each other’s fathers called out across the gap to men in the tents, sometimes to insult them, sometimes just to say their names.
Three days.

Here is what three days does, and I am going to say it plainly because the rowzeh-khan said it plainly and I have never got it out of my head. On day one the mouth goes and you are aware of it constantly and it is merely miserable. By day two the children stop being noisy about it. Their crying changes register and then reduces, because crying costs water, and a body that is running out will stop paying for things. By day three the small ones have gone quiet and the quiet is the thing that breaks the adults, because a silent thirsty child is a child that has begun to make arrangements.
They dug a well inside the camp. It came up dry.
They sent men out at night in small parties down to the river and some of them got back with skins and some of them did not.

And the whole time — this is the part I could not hold in my head at fifteen and can barely hold now — the river was audible. It is not a small river. On a still night, six hundred metres, you can hear water.
They lay in those tents for three nights listening to it.

The rowzeh-khan stopped there. He always stops there. He does not go on to the ninth, not on the seventh night, because the rite has a calendar and the calendar is not negotiable and you get the thirst on the night the thirst happened.
He put the microphone down and it thumped.

And in the silence before the nowheh started, I heard something I have never been able to unhear, which is the sound of four hundred men in a walled yard in south Tehran, in winter, all swallowing at the same time.

Then somebody at the back stood up and began handing out plastic cups of water from a crate, because that is what we do, that is exactly what we do on the seventh, we hand out water — and every man there took one, and drank it, in the dark, on the night the water was cut.
That is the rite. That is the entire rite in one gesture and it took me six more years to understand what it was doing to us.
You are given the water.
You drink it.
You are not Abbas. You never were. You are one of the eighteen thousand who wrote letters and stayed home.
PART THREE — THE WATER CUT
15. THE NIGHT — the sixth night, and the water
After the seventh chapter of the story is told, the street changes. Not the heyat. The street.
Somebody puts out a sabil [sa-BEEL].

A sabil is a water station and the word comes from the Arabic for a road or a way — something set on the road for whoever is passing, free, no counting. A folding table, a barrel, plastic cups in a sleeve, a boy of about nine whose entire job is refilling the sleeve. Sometimes a length of hose from a shop’s tap. Sometimes just a woman standing in a doorway with a tray.
There are four of them between our building and the main road. Four, in three hundred metres, in the coldest month of the year, in a country where nobody is thirsty.
You take one. You always take one. Refusing a sabil is not rude in the ordinary way, it is closer to refusing to shake a hand at a funeral, and I have never once seen anybody do it.
And after the seventh night I cannot stop seeing them.

Ice on the top of the barrel at ten at night. Cups in the gutter, hundreds, flattened, moving very slightly in the wind. A man tipping a whole cup out on the ground because he only wanted a mouthful. A child filling one, drinking half, filling it again. All month, in every direction, water being handed to people who do not need it, in the name of people who needed it and did not get it.
I ask Mehran about this on the way down.
I say, doesn’t it seem —
He waits.
I say, we hand it out because they didn’t have any.
He says, yes.
I say, so we’re doing the opposite of the story.
And he stops walking, which for him is not nothing, and he stands in the cold with his hand flat on the shutter of the bakery and gets his breathing organised, and then he says:
That’s correct. That’s the point. You do the opposite so that the doing of it hurts.
I did not understand him. I nodded like I did. He knew I hadn’t.
16. THE PLAIN — the eighth of Muharram, and the offer
On the eighth, or possibly the ninth, a man rode out from the army with a paper and stopped in front of the tents and called four names.

The commander who came was called Shemr [SHEMR], and he is the closest thing the story has to a villain who behaves like one, and the reason he came is small and domestic and awful. Hossein’s brother Abbas, and Abbas’s three full brothers, had a mother from the tribe of Kalb. Shemr was Kalbi. They were, in the arithmetic of that world, his people.
So he brought an aman [a-MAAN]. A safe conduct. A written guarantee of protection. Not for the camp. For four men.

He called their names across the open ground and told them they were not included in what was going to happen. He told them their sister’s sons and their brother’s children were a separate matter, but they themselves could walk out.
There is a version where Abbas answers with a speech. There are always versions with speeches. The oldest accounts are plainer and worse.
He said, may God curse you and curse your safe conduct. You would give us protection and give none to the son of the Prophet?
Then he turned his back on the paper.
I want to sit inside that for a second, because at fifteen I did not, and a rowzeh-khan will not let you.

They were offered a way out by name. Not a general amnesty they’d have had to trust. A specific document with their specific names on it, brought by a relative, delivered in daylight in front of witnesses, at a point when there was still water in the skins.

Everything that happens to Abbas after that — everything, the river, the hands, all of it — he chose on the eighth, in advance, with the exit standing right there in front of him holding a piece of paper.
That is why he is not simply a brave man in this story. Bravery is a thing that happens to you in a moment. Abbas had two days to reconsider.
17. THE NIGHT — the seventh night, and the alley
The seventh night I go out early.

That is unusual and I notice it even while it’s happening, which is a strange thing to be able to say. Normally it comes at the end of the shoor, in the last half hour, when everything is already destroyed. This time it comes in the second hour, in the middle of the latmiyeh [lat-mee-YEH], on the slow beat, and it comes hard, the way a foot goes through a stair.

The boy below is in the second row and the yard is packed to the gate. There is snow starting, the fine dry kind that does not settle, going sideways under the bulbs. The steam off four hundred men is coming up through the tarpaulin tear.
And then it moves.
That has never happened. In six years it has never once moved. I go up and I stay up, directly above, like something on a string. That is the whole architecture of it.

But this time it goes sideways, over the wall of the yard, over the roof of the shop, over the main road with the black banners across it, and it keeps going for what would be three streets if I were walking, and then it stops.

There is an alley. It is narrow enough that a car could not get in and a motorcycle would have to fold its mirrors. There are steel gates on both sides, painted, one green, one that was blue. There is a drain in the middle of the ground and the ground slopes to it.
A man is lying on the ground with his head lower than his feet because of the slope. He is wearing black, which tells me nothing, because everyone is wearing black.

There are five or six men standing around him. They are standing the way men stand when they are waiting for someone else to speak. One of them has both hands on top of his own head, fingers laced, elbows out. One is looking at the gate. Nobody is kneeling. Nobody is touching him.

The ground around his head is wet and going out toward the drain in a shape like a hand. It is not steaming. That is the detail. It is cold enough that night that everything steams — the men steam, the pots steam, my own breath steams — and what is on the ground is not steaming, which means it has been there a while.

I come back so fast that I go down on one knee and the man behind me hauls me up by the arm of my jacket without breaking rhythm, because that is the arrangement, and I get back on the beat because my row depends on my timing.
But I am not there for the rest of it. I am in that alley for the rest of it.

Afterwards, in the break, with the tea and the sugar and everybody’s ears ringing, I go and find Agha Sadegh, because he is old and because he counts out the chains and because at fifteen those two facts made him an authority on the invisible world.
I tell him what I saw. Not all of it. The alley, the man on the ground, the men standing.
And his face does something that I read, at the time, as awe.
He puts his hand on the back of my neck and he says, God is generous. God is very generous to you.
I say, but where was it?
He says, Karbala. Where else.
And I say, it didn’t look like Karbala.

And he smiles and he says the thing that everybody in that yard would have said, the thing that is the most beautiful sentence in our entire tradition and also the most useful sentence anybody ever handed a frightened child:
Every land is Karbala, pesaram. Every land.

I went home happy. I want that on the record. I walked home through the snow beside my uncle with my back opened up and my throat gone and I was happy, because a man with white in his beard had told me I was being shown things.
Agha Sadegh had put his hand on the back of my neck. I thought that was tenderness.
He was turning me to face the other way.
18. THE PLAIN — the night of the ninth
On the ninth the army moved forward and the camp asked for one night.
Just that. One night. Give us tonight and we will answer in the morning. And they got it, and what they did with it is the reason this story survived.

They spent it praying, and mending, and sharpening. The sound of the whetstone in the tents on the ninth is a fixed feature of every telling I have ever heard. A camp of seventy-two men in which almost everyone is a cousin, sharpening.
And at some point in that night Hossein gathered them and had the lamp put out.
That is in the accounts and it is the finest piece of engineering in the entire story. He had the light put out before he spoke, so that nobody would have to be seen while deciding.

Then he told them: they want me. Only me. The night will hide you. Take my family’s hands and go out into the dark, each of you take one of them with you, and get away, because these people will not pursue you once they have me.
Then he waited in the dark.
Nobody moved.

His brother Abbas spoke first, and then the others, one after another in the dark where their faces could not be checked, and one of them said the thing that I think about more than any other line in the whole of it. He said: if you killed me and then brought me back to life and killed me again, seventy times, I would not leave you.
And another said, plainly, without decoration: we stay so we are not ashamed.
There is one more thing about that night and it is the thing they do not put in the pamphlets.
They knew. Every adult in those tents knew what the next day was. They had the information, they had the darkness, they had the exit, and they had until dawn.
And they used the time to sharpen.

Nobody in that camp was surprised on the tenth. Which means nothing that happened the next day was a tragedy in the way a train crash is a tragedy. It was a decision, made in the dark, with the lamp out, by people who were given the chance to be cowards privately and passed it up.
That is what you are mourning. Not that they died.
That they saw it coming and stayed.
19. THE NIGHT — the eighth night, and asking
I try twice on the eighth. I want that noted, because for years afterwards I told myself I never asked anybody, and that is not true. I asked twice and I was answered twice and the answers were kind.
The first is Mehran, in the morning, over bread and cheese and the sound of his chest.
I say, when you were at the front, did you ever see things.
He says, everyone saw things.
I say, no, like — from above. Like you were up.
And he stops chewing. He genuinely stops. And he says, from above.
I say yes.
He says, who told you about that.

Which is not an answer to my question, it is a different question entirely, and I was fifteen and did not hear the difference. I said nobody told me anything, and he looked at the table for a while and then he said, eat, you’ll be standing all night.
That’s the first one. That’s my uncle, who loved me, given a clean shot at it three days before everything, and what he did was ask who told me, and then tell me to eat.
I have decided not to hold that against him. It took me a long time.
The second is Haj Nemat, in the shop, in the afternoon.

The shop is worth describing because I was in it constantly that month and because of what it becomes. White tiles to shoulder height, grey above. A rail across the back with the hooks on it. Sawdust on the floor in the morning and by evening the sawdust has been walked into a paste at the door and is clean again by the following morning, because he does that himself, last thing, alone.
He is boning out a shoulder when I come in and he does not stop while I talk, and the not stopping is what gives me the courage.
I tell him about the alley. All of it this time. The green gate, the drain, the slope, the men with their hands on their heads, the blood not steaming.

The knife keeps going. Nemat’s hands are the best hands I have ever seen do anything. There is no waste in them at all. He takes the blade around the blade bone in one movement and the meat comes off the way a coat comes off a chair.
Then he says, without looking up: describe the gates again.
I do.
He says: one green, one that was blue.
I say yes.
And he puts the knife down.

He puts it down flat on the block and he stands there with both hands on the edge of the block and his back to me, and he stays like that for what I would now estimate at four seconds and what felt at the time like a change of season.
Then he turns around and his face is completely pleasant.
He says, God is showing you Karbala. It’s a gift. Don’t chase it and don’t talk about it, because if you talk about it people will start expecting things from you, and then it stops.
I say, but it looked like —
He says, Ali jan. Every land is Karbala.
The same sentence. From the second man in two days. Word for word.
I have thought a great deal since about the fact that they had a sentence ready.
Then he does something that at the time was simply the best moment of my year.
He wipes his hands and goes to the back and comes out with a bundle wrapped in newspaper and puts it on the block and opens it, and it is the standard.

The alam. The word means a sign, a marker, a banner — the thing you can see from far away that tells you where your people are. Abbas carried the standard at Karbala, which is why the alam is Abbas, and why on the ninth night the man playing Abbas carries it.
It is brass and steel, about my height, with a hand at the top. A metal hand, palm out, fingers together. Everyone knows what the hand means and nobody says it.
He says, it’s heavier than it looks. Practise with it. If you drop it in front of four hundred people you will remember it when you’re sixty.
I take it. It is not heavier than it looks. It is lighter.
I did not notice that until I was twenty-one.
20. THE PLAIN — the ninth night, laying the table
On the ninth night the rowzeh-khan does not start where he left off.

He starts at the beginning. Every heyat does this and I have never heard anyone explain why, but the reason is obvious once you have stood in the yard on a ninth night: the yard is full of strangers. All month it is the same three hundred men. On the ninth and the tenth it is everybody — the ones who come twice a year, the boys from other streets, the ones who have not been inside the gate since their father died. So before he takes them into the worst day, he lays the table.

He does it the way you would tell a child, and nobody in the yard is insulted, because everybody there has been told it a hundred times and everybody there still needs it. This is a thing I have not found anywhere else. A room of grown men letting themselves be told, slowly, from the top, something they have known since before they could read.
So. From the top.
Mohammad [mo-ham-MAD] is the Prophet. He has a daughter, Fatemeh.

Fatemeh marries Ali, who is the Prophet’s cousin, and who is the first Imam — the first of the line of guides that our half of Islam follows, and the reason our half is called what it is. Ali is my name. It is also every third man’s name in this country, for exactly this reason.
Fatemeh and Ali have two sons: Hassan [ha-SAN] and Hossein. These are the Prophet’s grandsons. He carried them in the street. Old men in Medina remembered it.
Hassan is the second Imam. He makes a treaty with Mo’aviyeh in Damascus and steps back from the fight, and he dies, and there are ugly stories about how.
Hossein is the third Imam. Hossein is who this month is about. He is fifty-six in the year 680.
Mo’aviyeh dies and his son Yazid takes the seat and demands the pledge. Hossein refuses and leaves Medina.
Now the family, because on the tenth you need to know who everybody is or the day is just a list.

Zaynab is Hossein’s sister. Full sister — same mother, Fatemeh, same father, Ali. She is older than he is. She is not going to fight. She is going to survive, and that turns out to be the harder assignment.

Abbas is Hossein’s brother, but a half-brother — same father, different mother. He is thirty-four. He is enormous. He carries the standard. His mother’s tribe is the reason Shemr comes out with the safe conduct, and the reason he refuses it.
Ali Akbar [a-LEE AK-bar] is Hossein’s eldest son. Eighteen. The family say he looks and sounds like the Prophet, which is a compliment that becomes unbearable later in the day.

Ali Asghar [a-LEE AS-ghar] is Hossein’s infant son. Asghar means the smaller. Akbar means the greater. Two sons, the same first name, sorted by size, and that is not a poetic device, that is simply what people did.

Zayn al-Abidin [ZEYN al-aa-be-DEEN] is another son, in his twenties, and he is lying in a tent with a fever so bad he cannot stand. Remember him. He is the only male over the age of childhood who is going to walk off that plain alive, and he lives because he is too ill to be worth killing.
Qasim [GHAA-sem] is Hassan’s son. Hossein’s nephew. Thirteen.
On the other side: Ebn-e Ziad in Kufa, who writes the orders. Omar son of Sa’d, who commands the field and does not want to. Shemr, who does.
And the last one, the one the rowzeh-khan always saves:
Hurr. The commander of the thousand cavalry who cut them off from the road on the way in. The man Hossein watered.
Then he goes into the morning of the tenth, and the first thing that happens on the morning of the tenth is Hurr.

He sat on his horse in front of his own thousand men and he began to shake. Visibly. A man beside him said something about it, said something like, you’re the bravest man in Kufa, what is this. And Hurr said: I am putting myself between heaven and hell and I am choosing.
Then he rode across the open ground alone.
He got down off the horse in front of the tents with his face in the dirt and said, I am the one who blocked your road. I am the one who brought you here. Is there repentance for me.
And Hossein said yes, and told him to stand up.
Hurr asked one thing. He asked to be the first to go out.

They let him. He was killed in the first half hour, and they carried him back into the tents, and Hossein wiped the dirt off his face with his own hand and said: you are free, as your mother named you. Because hurr means free. His name had meant that his entire life and he had spent thirty years being a professional soldier of the government and it had never once been true until that morning.
That is the first death of the day. That is where they choose to start it.
A man who was on the wrong side for the entire story and changed his mind with two hours left.
21. THE NIGHT — the other side of the curtain

I have been writing as though this month belongs to men, and I have been doing it because I was fifteen and a boy and stood where boys stand, and that is exactly the mistake I want to correct now, because it is the mistake the whole outside world makes about us.
What you see from the street is men. Rows of them, bare-armed in winter, chains going, blood on white cloth, drums. That is what the cameras take and it is what people mean when they say Muharram.
It is perhaps a third of it. Possibly less.
Start with a fact that took me years to be able to state plainly: almost nothing in that yard would have happened without women, and almost none of them were in it.

Three cauldrons. Four hundred families fed for two days on the ninth and tenth, and a smaller pot going every single night for ten nights. Rice, split peas, dried lime, onion, four sheep. Somebody has to clean three hundred kilos of rice. Somebody has to peel onions in a quantity that is not a domestic quantity, it is an industrial one, and somebody has to do it in a kitchen the size of a normal kitchen, over three days, standing.
That was done in the house behind the shop and in four other houses on our street, by somewhere between twenty and thirty women, some of whom were older than Agha Sadegh.
And when the food went out into the street at three in the afternoon on Ashura, it went out in the hands of men, and every photograph of it that exists is of men.
I said something about that once, at fourteen, in the kitchen, being useless with a knife. Something clever. Something along the lines of you do all of it and they carry it out.
And a woman called Mahin [maa-HEEN] Khanom [KHAA-nom], who was about sixty and had forearms like Haj Nemat’s, did not stop what she was doing and said:
Whose vow is it?
I did not understand.
She said: your uncle’s? Nemat’s? Whose vow do you think is in that pot?
She said: I vowed that. When my daughter was sick in Mordad [mor-DAAD]. I vowed it and I paid it and I cooked it and if you think the payment is the carrying, then you have understood nothing at all.
That is the first thing. The nazr [NAZR] — the vow — is disproportionately theirs.

A vow is a private contract with God and it has no ceremony and no witness and no clergy involved in it, and that means it is the one part of this entire religion that requires nobody’s permission. You can make one lying in the dark next to a sick child. You do not need a mosque and you do not need a man.

And so it is everywhere among women in this country, and it is enormous, and the entire economy of Muharram — the food, the tea, the sugar, the black cloth, the candles, the money that is quietly put into Nemat’s hand and never counted out loud — is very substantially a settlement of debts that women incurred alone at three in the morning.
Second thing. They have their own rooms.

There is a curtain in the yard and I have walked past it for six years and never once looked at what is behind it, because I was fifteen and it did not occur to me that there was anything behind it except my mother’s absence.
What is behind it is a mourning gathering with its own structure, its own reciter, its own economy and its own emotional rules, and those rules are not the men’s rules.

There are rowzeh-ye zananeh [row-ZEH-ye za-naa-NEH] — women’s rowzeh — held in houses, in the afternoons, all month, and in many neighbourhoods every week of the year. A woman comes and recites. She is paid. She is often extremely good and sometimes she is locally famous and this is a real profession that has existed for centuries and has no male equivalent in the domestic setting.
There is the sofreh [sof-REH], which means a cloth spread on the floor for eating, and which in this context means a votive gathering

— a cloth is laid, specific foods are put on it in specific numbers, the story is told, and the gathering is dedicated to a particular figure. The sofreh of Abolfazl — which is Abbas — is the most common of all, and it is for things that are asked for and things that were granted, and it is run entirely by women, in a house, for women.
And they beat their chests. That surprises people. Not in rows, not with chains, but on the same beat, a hand on the chest, for as long as the men do.
Third thing, and this is the one that reorganised my understanding of the entire month.
The men resemble the dead. The women resemble the survivors.
Look at what the story actually offers each side.

A boy in that yard is offered Abbas, Ali Akbar, Qasim, Hurr, Hossein. Every single one of them dies. The whole male catalogue is a set of ways to be killed well, and a boy grows up choosing between them the way a boy elsewhere chooses a footballer.
And what is offered to a girl?

Zaynab, who watched every man she was related to killed in one afternoon, and was robbed, and roped, and walked eight hundred kilometres, and stood in two hostile courts and spoke, and lived for years afterwards.

Rabab [ra-BAAB], who was Ali Asghar’s mother, and who handed her six-month-old to his father to be carried out into the open, and who is said afterwards to have refused shelter and sat out in the open ground of Karbala for a year.
Roqayyeh [ro-ghay-YEH], three or four years old, going body to body in the dark looking for her father.
Sakineh [sa-kee-NEH], Hossein’s small daughter, who is remembered mostly for what happened to her afterwards, in captivity, in the dark part of the road.
Not one of them dies on the tenth. Every one of them has to keep going after it.

So the men in that yard spend ten nights rehearsing how to die, and the women in the house behind it spend ten nights rehearsing how to survive somebody, and I would like anyone who thinks this is a male ordeal to sit down and decide honestly which of those two is the harder rehearsal.
The fourth thing happened on the seventh day and I have never been able to write about it without stopping.
There is a ceremony that had only existed for about a year by then. It started in 1381 — 2003 — and it went through the country like weather, and by 1382 our neighbourhood was doing it.
It is for Ali Asghar, the infant.

And what it is, is this: on the seventh day of Muharram, mothers come, and they bring their babies. Hundreds of them. Thousands, in the big halls. Every infant is dressed in a small white shroud, or in green, with a headband, and the mothers sit on the floor holding them.
And a reciter tells the story of a six-month-old carried out into the open ground and held up to be seen.
And at the moment in the telling where the arrow comes, every mother in the room lifts her own child.
Up. In two hands. Into the air.
Our street did it in the mosque hall because the yard was not for women. I did not see it. I was fifteen and male and I was outside on the step with the other boys and the door was shut.
What I got was the sound.

I have heard a great many sounds in yards and halls in this country. I have heard six hundred ruined throats on a tenth night. I have heard four hundred men make a noise like a building settling when a boy pours water back into a river.
The sound that came through that door was not related to any of them.

It was hundreds of women in a room, all at once, and underneath it — because you cannot lift a sleeping baby into the air without waking it — hundreds of babies, and the babies were the top of the sound.
I sat on a step in the cold and did not know what to do with my face.
I asked Mahin Khanom about it, years later, on a bad line, from Los Angeles.
I said: why would you do that. Why would any mother in the world do that on purpose.
And she said — and I have not improved on it in a decade of thinking —
She said: because every one of us is going to hold something up one day and not get it back. That is not a story, that is a certainty, that is simply what having a child is.
She said: so we do it once a year, on purpose, in a room full of women who are doing it at the same time, with the doors shut.
She said: your uncle had to carry it out of a marsh at twenty years old on his own in the dark. We do ours together, for two minutes, in the afternoon, with tea afterwards.
She said: which of us do you think is doing this correctly?
And the last thing, and this is where it stops being general and becomes mine.
Sohrab’s mother made the nazri.
Every year of my life. She was one of the twenty. She was the one who did the dried limes, because there is a way of cracking them so they open without shattering and she had it.
And in the year 1382, on the seventh day of Muharram, in the mosque hall, she was in that room.
Her own son had been dead for eleven months and the entire street had agreed to say he was in Dubai and she had agreed to it too, out loud, to neighbours, in a shop, for eleven months.
And she sat on a floor with the other women and listened to a man tell the story of a mother handing over a child.
And when they lifted, she had nothing in her hands.
Nobody in that room did not know.
Nobody in that room said anything.
That is what women do at Muharram, in case you were wondering whether they were merely catering.
22. THE NIGHT — Tasu’a, the yard, the animals

The ninth is called Tasu’a [taa-soo-AA], which is just the Arabic word for nine. Nothing more elegant than that. The tenth is Ashura, which is ten. Our largest days are named after where they fall in a row.
Tasu’a is the day the animals come.

They arrive at six in the morning in the back of a Nissan pickup, four of them, and they are unloaded by being lifted by the fleece over the shoulder and set down on the concrete. They are not distressed. That surprises people who have never been there. They are on a street they don’t know, so they stand close together and look at things.
They are tied to the rail by the yard wall. And then — this is the part I want you to sit inside — they are fed and watered.

There is a green plastic bucket. There is a hose. Haj Nemat fills the bucket and puts it down and the sheep drink, and they drink for a long time, the way sheep do, with a lot of noise and a lot of dropping back out of the sides of the mouth.
It is a rule. You do not slaughter a thirsty animal. You water it first and you feed it first and you do not sharpen the knife where it can see, and you do not slaughter one in front of another one.

I have heard these called mercies my whole life. They are in the books as mercies. And I have never been able to get past the following fact, which arrived in my head on that specific morning while I was holding the bucket, and never left:
We are three days into telling ourselves about children who died with no water, on a plain, six hundred metres from a river.
And we water the sheep first.
I am fifteen and it is my second year holding.

Holding is exactly what it sounds like. Two of us on the body, one at the head. You get the animal down onto its side — you do not throw it, you fold it, you take the legs and it goes down almost politely — and then you lie half across it and you take the two legs nearest you, one in each hand, and you brace.
Nobody explains any of this. You learn it by being the boy who is nearest when somebody says come here.

The word for the whole business is qorbani [ghor-baa-NEE], and here is the thing about that word. It comes from an Arabic root, q-r-b, and that root means nearness. Approach. To draw close. A sacrifice is not, in the language, a destruction. It is a closing of distance. You open a throat in order to get nearer to something.
I did not know that at fifteen. Mehran told me at some point that winter and I remember thinking it was one of his war things.
Here is what happens, and I am not going to arrange it.

Nemat kneels at the head. He turns the head toward the south-west, toward Mecca, with one hand under the jaw. He says the words, which take about two seconds, and the words are a permission and an announcement of who this is for.
The knife is long and thin and he sharpened it in the shop twenty minutes ago behind a closed door.

The cut is one movement and it is much deeper than you expect. It is not a slit. It goes through everything at the front of the throat down to the bone, both sides at once, and the noise is not a cry, because you have just removed the animal’s ability to make a cry. The noise is air. It is a wet ragged air noise out of the cut end of the windpipe and it goes on for longer than you have prepared yourself for, and it comes in a rhythm, because the animal is still trying to breathe, and it will keep trying for a while.

The blood does not spray. That is television. It comes out in a heavy dropping surge in time with the heart, and there is a great deal of it, and it is very hot. On an Esfand morning it steams. It steams enormously. There is a cloud of it coming off the concrete.

The legs in my hands go rigid and start to kick. Not weakly. This is where the boy is needed. It is not distress, they tell you, it is nerves, the animal is already gone, and I do not know if that is true and I do not think anybody holding the legs believes it while it is happening.
I have my face about forty centimetres from the fleece of its ribs and I can feel the heart under my chest through my coat, going hard, then going wrong, then going small.
Then it stops and the legs go loose all at once, and the loose is worse than the rigid, and you let go and stand up and your knees are wet.
The blood runs to the drain. It goes in a hand shape.

By ten there are four of them hanging on the rail and the yard smells like a coin held in a fist. The skins come off in that way where it is a wrestle at the start and then it is a zip. The heads are on the concrete facing different directions with their eyes open and a boy of about seven is squatting looking into one of them very calmly.
At eleven the cauldrons go on.

By two in the afternoon the whole street smells like gheimeh [ghey-MEH] — split peas, dried lime, onion cooked down to nothing, meat that was warm this morning — and it is the best smell in the world. I want to be precise. Not a good smell. The best smell in the world.
And I am fasting, or half-fasting, the way you do, and I have been up since five, and my mouth is running water.
I look at the drain. I look at the pot. My mouth is running water.
Whatever a person is supposed to be at fifteen, that is what I was, and none of it fitted together, and nobody in that yard had ever suggested that it was supposed to.
The reason for all of it, if you ask, is nazr.

A vow. Somebody’s wife was ill. Somebody’s son had the medical exams. Somebody was in a car that should have killed him on the Karaj [ka-RAJ] road and was not. And in the moment of it they said: if this goes the way I am asking, I will feed the street on Ashura.
And it went the way they asked. And now there is a debt, and the creditor is not a person, and cannot be paid in money, and does not send letters.

So you pay it in meat. And you give the meat away — that is the whole mechanism, that is the load-bearing wall. It is called nazri and you may not sell it, you may not keep the good part, you may not check who is taking it. A man in a suit takes a portion and a man who sleeps under the flyover takes a portion and neither of them is asked anything at all.
There is one more layer and Mehran gave it to me that afternoon with a bowl in his hand.
He said: you know why a sheep, and not money.
I said no.

He said: because Hossein is called the slaughtered one. The one who was offered. There’s an old story where a father is told to sacrifice his son and at the last second a ram is sent instead and the son is spared. Everybody has that story.
He drank some tea. He said:
At Karbala nobody sent the ram.
23. THE PLAIN — the tenth, the young men
They came out one at a time, because that was the form.

Single combat first, which sounds antique and was in fact simply the procedure, and the seventy-two were very good at it, and for the first part of the morning the arithmetic did not look like arithmetic. Then Omar son of Sa’d stopped allowing it, because he could count, and after that it was volleys and mass and it stopped being combat.

Qasim was thirteen. Hassan’s son. There is a tradition, and it is a tradition rather than a certainty, that his marriage to one of Hossein’s daughters was performed in the camp during the fighting — an hour of a wedding in a tent with an army outside — and this is the single most theatrical thing in the whole story and every heyat in Iran does it and there is not a dry face in the yard when they do. He asked his uncle three times for permission to go out. Three times he was refused. The fourth time Hossein could not refuse him. He was trampled by horses.

Ali Akbar was eighteen and the family said he had the Prophet’s face and the Prophet’s voice. He asked, and his father gave permission, and then his father stood and watched him ride out and said, to nobody, and it is recorded: the most like him in face and speech, and when we longed for the Prophet we would look at this boy.
He was speared and the horse carried him back and he was brought into the tents and his father put his own cheek against the boy’s cheek.
That is the thing they use. Not the spear. The cheek.
I want to say something about how this lands in a yard, because from outside it must look like professional grief. It is not.

By the time the rowzeh-khan reaches Ali Akbar on the ninth night, every man in there is somewhere else. A man is crying about a boy from Karbala and he is also crying about his own son, or his brother from the war, or the one who went to Sweden and does not call. There is a doorway in the story and the story keeps it open on purpose. That is the function.
I looked around that night and understood, for the first time, that not one of these men was crying about the year 680.
I thought I was the exception. I thought I was the one who was properly there, in the desert, doing it correctly.
I was in an alley three streets away, and I did not know that yet, and I had thirty hours left of not knowing it.
PART FOUR — THE ROLE
24. THE NIGHT — the ninth night, the resemblance

The play is not called a play. It is called shabih-khani [sha-BEEH-khaa-nee], and that means resemblance-reading, and I have thought about that phrase more than about almost any other words in my language.

The polite word is ta’ziyeh, from the Arabic for condolence, and that is the word the newspapers use and the word on the sign at the cultural centre. But the old word, the one Agha Sadegh uses, is shabih. Resemblance. And it does not mean you are acting a person. Acting is a lie that everyone has agreed to. A resemblance is not a lie. A resemblance is a claim that for a short time, in poor light, in a small yard, this is the closest thing available.
They clear a space against the wall. That is the stage. There is no stage. There is a space and a bulb.

There are no costumes to speak of. Green for the family. Red for the army. If you are playing a woman you are a man in black with your face covered, and nobody laughs, ever, not once, not in the history of this country.

And there are no memorised lines. This surprises people. You hold your lines in your hand on a strip of paper called a tumar [too-MAAR] and you read from it in front of everybody, and the reading is not a failure of the performance, it is the performance. Because the moment you memorise it you are pretending to be him. Holding the paper means you are not him. It means you are a butcher’s nephew from Nazi Abad with a piece of paper, resembling.
They put the green over my shoulders and it smells of the trunk.
I have the alam in both hands and it is lighter than it looks and I have not thought about that once.
And the yard is packed to the gate and out into the passage and there are men standing on the wall.
Here is what the scene is. It is short. It is always the same. Abbas takes the empty waterskin and goes down to the river.
I walk the length of the carpet. Four hundred men are silent, which is a sound. Somebody at the back is already crying and the play has not started.
I kneel down at the place where the river is, which is a strip of blue cloth held at either end by two boys younger than me, and it is absurd, and it is not absurd at all.

I put the mashk [MASHK] into the river. The mashk is the waterskin — an actual one, old, stiff as a boot. It fills. Somebody with a jug behind the cloth makes it fill, and everybody knows that, and everybody has stopped breathing.
And then I do the thing.
I lift the water to my mouth in my cupped hands. I am supposed to. It is written on the paper in my hand. I lift it, and I hold it there, and I look at it.
And I put it back.

That is the scene. That is all of it. A man reaches water after three days of nothing and refuses it because there are children behind him who have none, and he pours it back out of his hands into the river.
The yard made a noise I had never heard four hundred men make. Not weeping. Something below weeping. A single low sound like a building settling.
There is a thing I did in that moment that I have never told anybody and that I am going to put down here because this book is worth nothing if I leave it out.
While the water was in my hands — while four hundred men were not breathing — I turned my wrists about ten degrees.
Because I had worked out, somewhere in the two seconds before, that from the third row back the water would not catch the bulb unless I turned them.

That is the first recorded instance in my life of me editing an event, while I was inside it, for the benefit of people who were not going to remember it. I was fifteen years old and I was standing in a resemblance of the worst afternoon in the history of my religion and I was managing the lighting.

I have done it in every important moment I have had since. I did it at my uncle’s grave. I did it in a federal building in Los Angeles with a man deciding whether I could stay in his country. I am doing a version of it now, in this paragraph, and I know I am, and I cannot get underneath it.
I was fifteen and I want to be honest about what I felt.
I felt magnificent.

Not moved. Not holy. Magnificent. I was the tallest thing in south Tehran. Men I had never spoken to were putting their hands flat on their own chests when they looked at me. Somebody’s mother was calling out a prayer from the women’s side of the curtain and it had my name in it.
I did not think about the water once. I thought about how it looked when I put it back.
That is the sentence, if you want the whole book in one. I performed the refusal of relief and enjoyed it enormously.
Afterwards, in the storeroom, taking the green off, Agha Sadegh is folding.
I say, was it right?
He says, it was right.
I say, was it better than —

And I stop. Because I do not have a name to put at the end of that sentence. I have never had a name to put at the end of it. I have spent nine days holding a part that somebody must have held before me and I have never once been told who.
Agha Sadegh keeps folding. He is very old and his hands are not good any more and folding takes him a while.
He says: don’t ask me that.
Not angry. Not sharp. Tired, and something else.
Then he says: ask me on the eleventh.
25. THE PLAIN — the river
By the afternoon of the tenth almost all of the men were dead and the children in the tents had not had water for three days.
Abbas took the waterskin.

He went alone, on horseback, in the direction of the Euphrates, and there were something in the order of four thousand men positioned between the tents and the water, and he went through them. That is what the accounts say and I have no way to improve on it. He went through them and got to the bank and got down and put the skin in the river and filled it.
Then he took water in his hands and lifted it to drink.
He had not had water for three days either. Nobody had. He was thirty-four years old and enormous and he had been fighting since morning in armour in Iraq, and he was standing in the river.

Thirty-four. I am writing this at thirty-four. I did not plan that and I noticed it about four pages ago and I have decided to leave it in, because leaving it in is the honest thing and because I have spent this entire book warning you about exactly the pleasure I just felt when I worked it out.
And he stopped.

The tradition preserves what he said to himself, and it is not a speech, it is a man arguing with his own hands. He said something to the effect of: my body, you are worthless. After Hossein you are nothing. He is thirsty and you would drink.
And he put it back.

He got up out of that river with an empty mouth and a full skin and started back with four thousand men between him and the tents, and now he could not fight properly, because he had one job, and the job was in his arms.
They came at him from the left and took his right arm off at the shoulder.
He moved the skin to the other arm and kept going.
They came at him from the right and took the left one.
He caught the strap of the waterskin in his teeth and kept going.
Then an arrow went into the skin, and the water came out of it, and he watched it come out.

They say the mace came down on his head after that, and that he called for his brother once, and that Hossein came out and found him and could not carry him back, and did not bring him back, and the reason given is that Abbas had asked him not to — because Abbas had children in that camp too, and one of them was standing at the tent flap watching the horizon.
That is why there are no hands on our standard. There is one hand, at the top, palm out.
That is why he is called Saqqa [sagh-GHAA]. The water-carrier. Not the standard-bearer, not the lion, not the brother. The water-carrier. He is named after the errand he failed.
And that is why my uncle refused to tell me and sent me to listen.
Because if you tell a boy Abbas got the water, he hears a man succeeding.
What actually happened is that a man reached the thing everyone in the world wanted, held it in his hands, put it back, and then lost both arms carrying it to children who did not get it anyway.
Nobody drank. That is the story. The water never arrived.
26. THE NIGHT — the tenth, before light
I cannot sleep and I do not try very hard.

It is about half past four and the shabih is six hours behind me and my back is stuck to my shirt in a way that is going to be interesting to undo, and I am lying on the floor of the front room listening to Mehran breathing through the wall, and the breathing is doing the thing it does at night, the long gaps and then the catch.
At five I get up and put my coat on over the shirt and go out.

Ashura morning at five in the morning in Nazi Abad in Esfand is a specific thing that I have not seen the equal of anywhere. The banners are up and there is nobody under them. The whole street is dressed and empty, like a hall after they have put out the chairs and before anyone comes.
It is maybe minus four. The gutters are frozen at the edges. There is a smell of the cauldrons which have been on since three.
And I walk, and I do not admit to myself where I am walking, which is a skill I have had my whole life and which has not served me well.
Down past the bakery. Across the main road. Past the mosque with the loudspeakers still bolted to the pole from last year. Left. Then the second right, which is not really a right, it is a gap.
And the alley is there.
It is there. That is the whole sentence.

It is about a metre and a half across. There are steel gates on both sides. One of them is green. The other one is a colour that used to be blue and has been sanded and primed in patches and never finished.
The ground slopes to a drain in the middle.
I stand at the mouth of it for a long time. Long enough that a woman comes out of a doorway behind me with a bag and looks at me and decides I am nothing, and goes.
Then I walk in and crouch down by the drain.

The concrete around it is a different colour. Not dramatically. It is the way concrete goes when something has been washed off it hard and repeatedly — a paler patch with a dark edge where the hose did not reach, in a shape that runs out from the drain like a hand with the fingers spread.

There is a thin dark line in the crack between two slabs that no amount of hose is going to get out, because concrete is porous, and I would not have known that at fifteen except that I had spent the previous morning holding sheep and had already learned that you can wash a yard for an hour and the cracks stay.
I am going to be exact about the next thirty seconds because they were the end of my childhood and I have gone back over them so many times that they are worn smooth.
First I thought: this is Karbala. Every land is Karbala. I have been shown a thing.
Second I thought: Karbala is a plain. Karbala is sand and a river and tents and forty thousand men. There are no steel gates in Karbala. There is no drain in Karbala. There is no hose.

Third I thought about the men standing with their hands laced on top of their heads, and I thought: nobody stands like that in a story. That is not how people stand in stories. That is how my uncle stood in the corridor of the hospital in Farvardin two years ago, the week my grandmother’s heart was being looked at, when they came out to talk to him.
And fourth — and this is the one, this is the hinge of my entire life — I thought:
I have been floating over the same place for nine nights and calling it the desert, and it is a hundred and eighty seconds from my house.
I put my fingers on the pale patch. It was concrete. It was cold. It was concrete.
Walking back the sun was not up but the sky over toward Rey had gone the colour of the inside of a wrist.
There was a man setting out a sabil at the corner. Folding the legs down on the table, sleeve of plastic cups, barrel.
He said, God accept it, agha.
He said it to me, because I was fifteen and in black with my collar wrecked and it was Ashura and I was clearly coming back from something.
He held out a cup of water.
And I took it and drank it, because what else does a person do, and it was so cold it hurt my teeth.
27. THE PLAIN — the infant
I am going to tell this one the way it was told to me, on the tenth day, at about eleven in the morning, in a yard that held six hundred people, by a man whose voice had already gone.
Everyone was dead.

Not the women. Not the children. The men. All of them, the seventy-two, the sons, the nephews, the brothers. Abbas in the river bed with the skin empty. Ali Akbar in the tent. Qasim under the horses. Hurr, first, hours ago, in the morning of a different life.
And Hossein was alone, and he was fifty-six, and he had been in the sun in armour since dawn.
He came out in front of the army and he asked for water for the children. Not for himself. He said it plainly. There is a baby in that tent.
They did not answer.
So he went back and he took the child out of the tent.
He was six months old. His name was Ali, and because there was already an older brother called Ali, they called this one Asghar, which means the smaller.
And Hossein carried him out into the open ground in his two hands and lifted him up so that the army could see him.

That is the whole gesture. He held him up to be seen. He turned so that the ranks could look at him. He said, if you have decided about me, this one has not decided anything. He has done nothing to you. He is thirsty.
There are thousands of men standing there.
And the accounts say a man named Hormola [hor-mo-LAA] put an arrow through the child’s throat while he was being held up.
Hossein caught the blood in his hand. He is described as holding his palm under it, and filling it, and then throwing it up into the air.
And there is a line that goes with that which is the reason my throat closes even now, and it is this: he said, it is easier for me because God is watching.
Then he went back and dug a small grave with his sword.

Here is the thing about that story that took me until my twenties to see, and I am putting it here rather than at the end because I want it standing next to what I had just found in an alley three streets from my house.
Ali Asghar was not killed because he was a threat. He was not a soldier. He was six months old.
He was killed because he was shown.
The father lifted the child up to be looked at, in order to make the crowd feel something, and the crowd felt something, and the something got the child killed.
Every man in that yard was weeping. Six hundred of them. My uncle was on a plastic chair at the back with his hand over his eyes and his chest going like a bellows.
And I was standing at the front, in the place where I always stood, where I had been put when I was nine, where four hundred men could see me.
Held up.
28. THE NIGHT — the marshes
My uncle went to the war at nineteen and came back at twenty-one with a chest that would kill him twenty years later, on an instalment plan, a little every winter.
He almost never talked about it. What he did instead — and I did not recognise this for what it was until I was much older — was talk about the water.
The place was called Majnoon.

It is a word that in Arabic and Persian means mad, or possessed, and it is the same word that gets attached to the lover in the old poem, the one who goes into the desert over a woman and forgets how to be a person. Majnoon and Leyli. Every child here knows it.

And by an accident that nobody planned, the largest oilfield in that war was called the Mad Islands, and tens of thousands of teenagers were fed into it over eight years, and now when an Iranian of a certain age says the word majnoon in a room, everybody knows which meaning is meant, and it is not the poem.

The islands were in the hoor [HOOR] — the marshes. Not a swamp in the way you are picturing. A shallow inland sea of reeds, thousands of square kilometres of it, water a metre deep and reeds four metres high, and channels through it that a man in a boat could get lost in for a week.
Mehran used to describe it and his whole face would change, and I want to be precise about this: it did not change into horror. It changed into something closer to homesickness.
He said: it was the most beautiful place I have ever been in my life and I will never forgive it.
He said the reeds moved all night. Not in a wind. Just moved, the way a crowd moves, and you learned very early not to look at them for too long.
He said the water at dawn went the colour of tea with milk in it.

He said there were birds in there in numbers that do not exist any more anywhere. He said that on one particular morning in the spring of 1365 — 1986 — something startled a flock off the water about two hundred metres from his position and it went up in a sheet, and it took, he said, ninety seconds for them all to get off the surface, and for ninety seconds nobody on either side of that marsh fired a shot.
He said: I was nineteen. I had been awake for two days. I stood up in a reed bed in the middle of a war and watched birds for a minute and a half.
Then he said, and this is the whole of my uncle in one sentence:
He said: and then somebody shot at us, and I got down, and that is the last time in my life I have ever been anywhere without wondering how long it was going to last.
The gas came in 1366.
He did not describe it as an event. He described it as weather, which I have since learned is how everyone who was there describes it.

He said you did not see it. In the reeds you did not see anything. What you got was a smell — and everybody says a different smell, garlic, geranium, cut grass, mustard — and his was geranium, which is a flower that grows in a pot on almost every balcony in this city, and which he could not be in a room with for the rest of his life.

He said the thing about that particular agent is that it is patient. It does not put you down. You smell geranium, and you think about it, and then you get on with the afternoon and you feel fine for two hours, sometimes six, and it is in that window that men do the fatal thing, which is nothing. They do not wash. They keep the clothes on. They lie down on the ground and sleep in it.
He said the ones who were quickest to wash lived best. That was the whole lottery. Not courage, not position, not luck in the ordinary sense.
Who washed.
He was in a reed bed. He was standing in water.
He said: I was luckier than any man I know. I was already standing in the only thing that could help me and I did not have to be told twice.

He came out of it with about a third of the lung tissue a man of that age should have, and the scarring goes on scarring, which is the part people do not understand — it is not an injury he received, it is an injury he continued to receive, quietly, every year, for two decades, from an afternoon in 1366.
And here is the thing I have to put down, because it is the reason my uncle is in this book and not merely in my life.
He learned to carry men out of that marsh.

There was no medic on his section for a period of some weeks and he was the one who had done a fortnight’s course in Ahvaz [ah-VAAZ], and so he became the one, at twenty, in reeds, in water up to the knee, with no light.
He put his hands inside three men that he told me about and there were others he did not tell me about.
Two of the three lived.
So when I say that in a yard behind a green gate at four in the morning in the year 1381, eleven men turned and looked at Mehran — understand what they were looking at.
They were looking at the only man in that yard who had ever had another man’s blood on his forearms in the dark and made a decision about it and been right.
They were not looking at a coward. They were not even looking at a bystander.
They were looking at the most qualified person available.

And he was thirty-five, and it was minus something, and he had a third of a set of lungs and about eight seconds, and he had spent fifteen years not being asked, and the one time in fifteen years that a room turned round and made him the medic again — he said wait.
I asked him once, later, in the last year, when he was on the oxygen and had stopped pretending about most things.
I said: if it had been the marsh. Twenty years old, in the reeds. Same wound, same night. What would you have said?
And he thought about it for a long time, which cost him, and then he said:

I would have said the same thing. That is what I cannot get past. I would have said the same thing and in the marsh I would have been right, because in the marsh there is no hospital forty minutes away and no telephone and no choice, and being right is easy when there is only one thing you can do.
He said: it was not the marsh, Ali. It was Nazi Abad. There was a hospital. There was a car and there was a telephone and there was a road.
He said: and I gave a marsh answer.
29. THE NIGHT — Ashura, the street, and the vans
By nine in the morning the street belongs to the dasteh [das-TEH].

A dasteh is a procession and the word just means a bunch, a handful, a group held together — the same word you would use for a bunch of keys. That is the correct amount of poetry for it. It is a handful of men held together, moving at walking pace, and there are five of them out that morning from five different heyats and they have to be timed so they do not meet, and the timing is a real logistical problem that real men have real arguments about in Azar.
Ours goes out at nine-thirty behind the drums.

The drum is a dohol [do-HOL] and it is the size of a table top and the man carrying it is walking backwards half the time so the rows can see the beat. There are cymbals — sanj [SANJ] — three pairs, and the sanj is the thing that gets into your skull, because a drum you feel and a cymbal you cannot get away from.
Twenty across, and however many rows deep, and every man’s zanjeer going right shoulder, left shoulder, on the beat.
From a rooftop it would look like one object breathing.
From inside it is four hours of the back of the head of the man in front of you.
At the top of the street where it meets the main road there are two vans parked with their back doors open and a table set up between them.
White vans. Red crescent on the side. A banner across the front of the table with a line of poetry about the blood of Hossein and, underneath it, in smaller letters, the opening hours.
Blood donation.

There is a queue. Not a small one. Forty men, maybe, some of them still in the black, some with their shirts obviously stuck to their backs, waiting on the pavement on Ashura morning to lie on a folding bed and have a needle put in and fill a bag with a barcode on it.
I stop and look at it long enough that Mehran, who is walking at the very back where he always walks, stops too.
He says, don’t stare.
I say, why is that there?
And he does the thing where he chooses.
He says: because they took the other thing away, and you cannot take a thing away from people. You can only put something in its place.
I say, what other thing.
And he starts walking again, at his own speed, which is the speed of a man with a third of a set of lungs going up a very slight incline, and he says, over his shoulder, in a completely flat voice:
Ask your friend Nemat.
That is the first time in my life that Mehran ever said Nemat’s name with anything in it.
30. THE PLAIN — the man who turned around
I want to tell you about Hurr, and I want to tell it properly, because he is the reason this story is a religion and not a war memorial.

Every year, on the tenth morning, the rowzeh-khan does not begin the day’s killing with Hossein and does not begin it with the children. He begins it with a middle-aged government soldier who spent the entire story on the wrong side.
That is a choice. Somebody made that choice, and kept making it, in every yard in this country for hundreds of years. And when you understand why, you understand what this month is actually for.
His full name was Hurr ibn Yazid al-Riyahi [HORR eb-ne ya-ZEED al-ree-yaa-HEE], and to be clear, the Yazid in his name is his own father and has nothing to do with the caliph; it was a common name.
Hurr means free. It is a word about status. In that world it meant a man who was not owned — not a slave, not a client of some larger man, a person whose word belonged to himself.
His mother named him that. It is the ordinary sort of hopeful thing a mother does.

And he then spent thirty-odd years being a professional cavalry officer of the government of Iraq, which is to say a man whose entire working life consisted of doing what a letter from Kufa told him to do.
Hold that. The whole chapter is in it.
He appears on the desert road with a thousand horsemen.

Here is his situation, and I want you to sit in it rather than watch it. He is a competent officer with orders. The orders are not kill anyone. The orders are administrative and they are, in their own terms, entirely reasonable: intercept this party, do not permit it to proceed to Kufa, do not permit it to return to Medina, hold it in open country, await instruction.
Nobody in the history of the world has ever been fired for carrying out an order like that.
And he rides all day in October heat to do it, and by the time he reaches the caravan his thousand men and their animals have not drunk since before dawn.
Then the man he has come to intercept looks at his horses and says: water them.
Consider what that does to a person.
Hurr was not a fool. He knew that the water in that caravan was finite, and that it was being poured into the mouths of the men who had come to trap them, and that Hossein knew it too.

And there is a detail in the accounts that is almost too much: where a soldier was too far gone to hold his own bowl, the people of the caravan held it for him and tilted it. Physically supported the head of a man sent to arrest them.
That is not diplomacy. Nobody was watching who mattered. It bought nothing.
Then the hour for prayer came, and Hossein asked Hurr whether he would pray with his own men or with the caravan.
And Hurr said: behind you.
A thousand government cavalry lined up behind the man they were detaining and prayed, and then got back on their horses and continued detaining him.
For four or five days after that they moved together and it is one of the strangest arrangements in any story I know.

Hurr did not attack. He did not permit them to leave the road he had put them on. When they turned toward one town, he moved to block. When Hossein spoke to his people, Hurr’s men sat within earshot and listened.
He was, in the plainest possible terms, doing his job to the letter while dying inside it.

And at Karbala, when the ground was chosen — and it was Hurr who did not let them go further — he stood there while a fifty-six-year-old man asked what the place was called, and heard him repeat it, karb and bala, grief and affliction, and heard him say put down the tents here.
Then the letters started arriving from Kufa and each one was worse than the last, and Hurr had to read them and pass them on.

Then the four thousand of Omar son of Sa’d [O-mar eb-ne SAAD] arrived, then more, then more. And on the seventh, Hurr watched five hundred cavalry ride down and stand between the tents and the river, and understood that there were fifty children in those tents.
He had three more days.
I want to say what is actually happening to him in those three days, because this is the part the rite is interested in and it is not the swords.
He is a man who has already done the wrong thing, and the wrong thing is now too large to undo, and every hour he stays makes it larger.

That is the most common human situation there is. It is more common than grief. Everyone reading this has been in some version of it — a job, a marriage, a silence, a thing you were part of and did not stop. And the arithmetic is always the same and it is always wrong in the same direction: the more you have already invested in being on this side, the more expensive it becomes to admit that this is the side you are on.

By the morning of the tenth Hurr has been standing next to it for eight days. Everyone he commands has seen him do it. Everyone in the enemy camp has seen him do it. If he turns now he does not merely change sides — he announces to four thousand men that he has spent eight days being the man who brought a prophet’s family to a place called grief and affliction and then blocked the road behind them.
And that is precisely, exactly, why the rite starts the day with him.
At dawn on the tenth, in the ranks, he began to shake.

That is the image. It is preserved in the oldest accounts and it has never been improved on: a senior cavalry officer sitting on a horse in front of a thousand men he commands, in full view, shaking so badly that the man beside him remarked on it.
And what the man said was not kind. He said something like: what is this? If I were asked to name the bravest man in Kufa I would have said you. What is this?
And Hurr said: I am putting myself between heaven and hell and I am choosing.
Then he said, and this is the line that undoes the yard every single year: and I will not choose anything over heaven, even if I am cut to pieces and burned.
He turned the horse.
He rode out across that open ground alone with his back to four thousand men.

Think about how long that ride takes. Six hundred metres of flat ground at a walk, because he did not gallop, because a man riding at a camp is a man attacking it. He had to go slowly, in silence, on the tenth morning, with everyone on both sides watching, knowing that any one of the archers behind him could end it and that some of them were his own.
And when he got there he got off the horse and put his face in the dirt in front of the tents.
He said: I am the one who blocked your road. I am the one who brought you to this place. I did not think it would come to this. Is there repentance for a man like me?
Now. This is the part I need a new reader to sit still for, because everything about this month is contained in the answer.
Hossein could have said many things. He could have forgiven him with a speech. He could have said something enormous.
What he actually said was: get up. Yes. God accepts repentance.
That is all. Flat. Administrative, almost. No sermon, no conditions, no probation.
A man who has personally caused the deaths that are about to occur asks whether it is too late, at the last possible hour, with nothing left to offer, and is told: no. Stand up.
And then Hurr asked for one thing. He asked to be the first man to go out.
Not to be forgiven quietly and stand at the back. He wanted to be first, in front of the same four thousand men, so that everyone who had watched him block the road would watch him do this.
They let him. He was killed inside the first hour.
And they carried him back into the tents, and Hossein knelt down and wiped the dirt off his face with his own hand and said:
You are Hurr, as your mother named you. Free.
Thirty years of a name that was not true, and two hours of it being true, and the two hours are what he is called by forever.
Here is why the tradition keeps him at the front of the tenth day, and this is the lesson, and every rowzeh-khan in this country knows it whether or not he has ever put it into words.
A mourning rite that only had martyrs in it would be useless.

Think about who is actually in that yard. Six hundred men, and the honest truth about six hundred men anywhere is that almost none of them are Abbas and almost none of them are Zaynab. They are the ones who signed the letter and stayed home. They are the ones who stood in the crescent not wanting to be the one who went. They are the village that waited three days and then came out and did the decent thing. They are, every single year, eleven men in a yard discussing it while somebody bleeds.
If the story only offered you heroes to fail to be, nobody would come back. You would sit in that yard once, measure yourself against a man who cut off his own arms carrying water, and never return.
So the story has a door in it.
The door is a middle-aged government employee who did the wrong thing for eight days for entirely defensible reasons, and turned around with two hours left, and was told get up and nothing else.
That is why he goes first on the tenth morning. Before the sons. Before the infant.
Because before you can grieve for people who were better than you, somebody has to tell you that you are still allowed in the room.
I did not think about Hurr at all when I was fifteen.
I thought about Abbas. Every boy thinks about Abbas. Abbas is the one with the arms and the river and the standard, and a boy hears that story and wants the part.

It took me until I was in my thirties, in another country, with two hands that do not close in the cold, to work out that the story had a man in it for me all along, and that he was not the one I had been given, and that he had been standing at the very front of the tenth morning every single year of my life while I looked straight past him.
31. THE PLAIN — the last hour
He was alone from about the middle of the afternoon.
Fifty-six years old, in the sun, in armour, no water for three days, everyone he had brought with him dead including the six-month-old.
And the army did not close.

That is the detail. Thousands of men in a crescent around one man who could barely lift his arm, and for a long time nobody moved, and the accounts say they were shouting at each other to go and none of them went, and the reason given in every telling I have heard is the same: each of them did not want to be the one who met the Prophet’s grandson on the Day of Judgement and had to explain.
So they stood and they waited for somebody else to do it.
Which is not a story about the year 680. That is a story about a Tuesday. That is a story about every corridor and every committee and every alley in the world.
Eventually somebody threw a stone. Then the volleys started, because volleys have no author.
He came off the horse.
And then the horse went back to the tents by itself.

Zoljanah [zol-jah-NAAH]. That is the name that survived, and it means something like the winged one, and it went back across that ground alone with an empty saddle, and the women came out of the tents when they heard it.

Every heyat in this country walks a horse in the procession on Ashura and I did not understand, until I was much older, why it was the horse and not the man. Why the empty saddle is the thing we walk down the street.
Because nobody in those tents saw him die.
They found out the way everybody finds out. Something came home without him.
Then they cut his head off, and the heads of everyone else, and put them on spears, seventy-two of them, and rode the horses back and forth over the bodies until there was nothing to bury properly.
And they set the tents on fire with the women and the children still inside them.

That is where the tenth day ends. Not with a death. With smoke going up off a camp at sunset, and a horse standing somewhere with nobody on it, and a boy of twenty-something with a fever lying in a burning tent unable to stand up.
32. THE NIGHT — the tenth, the shop, the word
The dasteh comes back at two and the nazri goes out at three and by five the yard is a wreck of paper dishes and by six they have swept it and by seven the tenth night is starting.
I go into the shop at about half past four, when it is empty, because I know he cleans then.
Haj Nemat is doing the block with a wire brush and a bucket.
I say, Haj Agha, what’s qameh-zani [gha-meh-za-NEE]?
He does not stop brushing.
He says, who said that word to you.
I say, nobody. I heard it.
He says, where.
I say — and this is the only lie I told anybody that entire month, and it was a stupid one, and he knew — I say, at school.
And he stops brushing.

He tells me. That is the surprising part. I had gone in expecting to be sent out and instead he wiped his hands and leaned on the block and told me, and he told me straight, and I have come to understand that he told me because he had already decided that the alternative was that somebody else would.
He said: a qameh [gha-MEH] is a blade. Short, heavy, single edge. Some men use a sword.

He said: you shave the head first. You make a small cut in the scalp, here — and he touched the top of his own forehead at the hairline — and then you go along with the flat of it, tapping, on the beat, and the cut opens more, and the head bleeds the way a head bleeds.

He said: it looks like a great deal more than it is. The scalp is full of vessels and they do not close, so half a cup of blood on a white shroud looks like a man dying, and mostly it is a man who will have a headache and a scab and a story.
He said: mostly.

And then he said the thing I did not expect, which is that he did it. For eleven years. He described the feeling with a precision that I have never heard him use about anything else. He said the moment the cold goes down the back of your neck and you understand that you are no longer negotiating with your own body.
I said, so where is it? Why haven’t I seen it?

And he said: it was forbidden. In seventy-three — that is 1994 in the other calendar — there was a ruling. Not a suggestion. A ruling, from the top, that this thing is forbidden, that it is not part of the religion, that it makes us look like savages to people who are already looking for a reason.
He said: and they were right. I want you to understand that I think they were right.
Then he put the brush down.

He said: do you know what it had turned into by the end? By year six it had stopped being about Hossein. I will say that in my own shop and you can tell anyone you like. It had become about which yard bled hardest.

He said: men counting. Men going back out into the street afterwards so the other heyats could see the shroud. A boy from Khani Abad who went too deep on purpose because the year before somebody had said his father went shallow.
He said: that is not mourning. That is a competition with a wound as the score.
And then he said the thing that I did not understand for six years and that I now think is the truest sentence anybody said to me that entire month:
A grief you can win is not a grief.
Then he picked the brush back up.
He said: and it stopped in the street. It did not stop.
I said, where does it happen.
And Haj Nemat, who had answered every single question I had asked him for nine days, looked at me for a long time with the wire brush in his hand.

And he said: Ali jan, I am going to tell you something and I want you to hear it as a man and not as a boy. There are places in this neighbourhood I will not take you. Not because I do not love you. Because I do.
And I said, that’s not an answer.
And he said, no. It isn’t.
I got as far as the door.
And he said, behind me: your grandfather did it.
I stopped.
He said, eleven years, before your father was born. He stood where you stand. And then he held the lamp for the better part of forty more.
And I said, without turning round, because I could not turn round: is that what —
And he said, no. No. That is not what happened to your grandfather.
Which was true, and which was the most enormous lie he ever told me, and both of those things are the case at once.
33. THE NIGHT — my grandfather, going back
He was born in a house four hundred metres from the yard.
That is the thing nobody in my mother’s family ever said in a full sentence, and it is the reason for everything in this book.

He was from down there. Abbas Shabani was born in Nazi Abad in 1288 to a man who made shoes, and he repaired sewing machines in a shop the width of a door for forty years, and he was good at it in the specific patient way that this country used to reward, and by the time his son was fifteen he had sold the shop and the two rooms above it and bought a house in Mirdamad, when Mirdamad was still half orchard, and moved his wife and his son and his two daughters north, and never once, in the north, stopped being a man from the south.
And every year, on the tenth of Muharram, before it was light, he took a bus back down and went through the gate of a yard behind a butcher’s shop, and after seventy-three, through the other one.

Fifty years. I want the number plain, because it is the only kind of fact about him I possess that nobody in my family has ever disputed. Fifty Muharrams, and the first part of them in the yard with the rest of the men, and the last part of them — the part nobody in Elahieh ever asked about — not doing it, holding the lamp, and the last two of them behind the gate.

My mother knew there was a morning in the year when her father-in-law was not at home. My grandmother knew. My father knew exactly, because he had been born four hundred metres from it and had left it at fifteen and had built himself, over years, a man who was from the north — an accent, a table, a wine cupboard, a wife’s family with a footballer at the lunch — and nobody in Elahieh ever asked him about the south, because nobody in Elahieh asks anybody about the south. That is the standard arrangement in a family like mine. Everybody knows there is a morning. Everybody elects not to ask.

There was no religion in the house in Mirdamad either. I want that understood, because a reader outside will assume that an old man who goes south with a lamp is a religious man, and he was not, or not in any way that a mosque would have recognised.
