He did not pray. He read the paper. He argued with the radio. If you had asked Abbas Shabani whether he believed any of it he would have looked at you for a long time and said something about the price of tomatoes, and his son, who was made the other way, would have laughed at you, and the laugh would have been genuine, and it would have been in the northern accent, which my father had built himself, over years, the way you build anything.

Once a year, before dawn, in the yard he was born beside, my grandfather stood at a gate and held a lamp for men who were doing a thing he had done himself, for eleven years, when he was about the age my father was that winter.
Fifty years.
I need to say what I think that was, and then I need to say why I cannot be sure.

I think he had come a certain distance from where he started — not far, not fast, a shop and then a house and then a son with a degree and a Steinway — and that he had done it without ever once building a man to do it in, which is the thing that separates him from his son, and that there was something in him that the house in Mirdamad had no room for, and no vocabulary for, and no permission for, and that once a year he took a bus twenty kilometres south and stood with it in the only place on earth where nobody would ask him a single question about it, among men who had known his father, who called him by a name nobody in the north used, in a yard where his accent, which he had never lost, was simply everybody’s accent.
I think he went home to it.
I think that is all it was and I think that is enormous.
And then, when I was six, he took me.

Left me at the corner with the baker’s boy for twenty minutes and came out with the lamp still in his hand and took me back up on the bus and delivered me to Elahieh in time for school and never said one word about it, and I have no memory of it, none, and I have his one habit and I did not know I had it.
He went south to go back to something.
I went south to become something.
He was going home.
I was going somewhere I had never been and calling it home, and dressing for it, and getting off the bus two stops early, and telling myself for six years that I was passing.
There is one more thing, and it is the reason this chapter is in this book.

When Haj Nemat put a nine-year-old at the front of the dasteh in the first week — a mute, well-dressed, obviously northern child with an accent like a radio announcer — he was not doing it because a boy who leaves his body fills a yard. He did not know that yet. Nobody knew that yet.
He did it because the boy was Abbas’s.

Everything that happened to me for the next six years — the front row, the light chain, the part of Abbas, four hundred and sixty-five thousandths of a second — all of it grew out of one afternoon in Aban 1376 when the news came south and a butcher stood in his shop and thought: that is the old man’s grandson. The little one.
They did not take me in because I turned up.

They took me in because he had been coming down for fifty years and had never once asked them for anything, and then he was dead, and his son — who had not been through that gate since he was fifteen years old — buried him in three days from a hall in Mirdamad with a hired washer and a hired reciter, and did not send word south, and there was a child.
That is what a heyat is. I have told you what it is twice already in this book and I did not have this part.
They were not adopting a stray from the north.
They were settling something.
34. THE NIGHT — fifty years
I have exactly four solid memories of him.

One is the smell of machine oil, which came off his hands and out of the drawer of the table in the courtyard in Mirdamad where he still, in his eighties, took apart things that did not need taking apart, and which I have never encountered anywhere since and would recognise in a second.
One is a plate of watermelon, cut in that courtyard, in August, with the seeds flicked at a wall.
One is a word.
And one I did not know I had until I was fifteen years old and standing at the mouth of an alley at five in the morning knowing which gate it was.
He died in Aban of 1376. He was eighty-eight. I was nine.

Nobody in my family has ever said the word for what happened to him and I am not going to say it here either, not out of cowardice, but because I have come to understand that the silence is itself the artefact and if I break it in a book I will have destroyed the thing I am trying to describe.

What I will say is this: for two years before he died he was going somewhere, a little further every season, and there was a doctor eventually and a piece of paper eventually and my grandmother put the paper in a drawer, and in the house in Mirdamad and the apartment in Elahieh the thing was referred to, when it was referred to at all, as his head. By the last winter he did not know my father. He knew me, sometimes, for a second, and then he would look at me with enormous courtesy, the way you look at a child somebody has brought to lunch. And then in Aban he died, in his own bed, with my grandmother holding his hand, and my father buried him in three days with hired men and did not send word south, and my mother took me to her sister in Karaj for a month, and I stopped speaking for six weeks, and my father tried once to say a word that had never been his and got one syllable of it out, and my uncle started coming up on Thursdays.
That is the whole of it. That is what a nine-year-old is given.

Agha Sadegh told me the rest in the hospital corridor about a week after my hands, sitting on a plastic chair with his stick between his knees, and he told it badly and out of order because he was eighty-one and in a hurry and it turned out he had about five months left.
He said: your grandfather did the qameh for eleven years, before your father was born, and he was the reason half of them did it.

He said: not because he was the loudest. Because he was the quietest. There are men who go into that yard to be seen doing it and there are two or three in every generation who go in the way a man goes into a room to put something down, and your grandfather was one of those, and the other men could tell, and they came because of him.
He said: and then he stopped, the year your father was born, because a man with a son does not, and he took the lamp instead, and he held it for the better part of forty years.
Then he told me what it was for, and I want to set it out carefully, because this is the part I did not understand until I was twenty-two and it reorganised my entire understanding of my own family.

He said: your grandfather had a thing in him. All the time. Every day of the year. He did not drink, he did not gamble, he did not shout at your grandmother, he did not hit anybody, he opened the shop at six and shut it at six and he was pleasant to everyone he met.

He said: and once a year, for about four minutes, before dawn, in a yard, he let it out. And when he stopped letting it out he stood at the gate and held a light for the men who were letting theirs out, and that was the same thing, and do not let anybody tell you it was not.
He said: fifty years. That is the entire account.
I said: and then?
And Agha Sadegh said: and then in seventy-three they forbade it.

Here is the thing that I have turned over for nineteen years and I am not going to pretend to have resolved it, because I do not think it resolves, and because the honest version has two halves that will not sit together.

The ruling was correct. I said that earlier and I will say it again in my own voice and not in Nemat’s: putting a blade into your own scalp is a bad thing to do, the ruling that stopped it was right on the medicine and right on the dignity and right on what it was turning into, and I would sign it today.
And.

There was a man in this city who had something in him that had no name, and no doctor, and no word, and no permission to exist at all, and there was exactly one arrangement in the entire world in which it was allowed out — once a year, at a fixed hour, in a walled yard, in front of witnesses who did not ask him a single question about it and never mentioned it for the other three hundred and fifty-four days.
And that arrangement was abolished, correctly, for excellent reasons, by people acting in good faith, and nothing was put in its place except a folding table with a barcode reader on it.
Agha Sadegh said: after that it went behind the gate.

He said: and behind a gate it is a different thing. In a yard with four hundred men and daylight coming and someone’s mother at the door with tea, it has edges. Behind a gate at four in the morning with eleven men who are all committing an offence, it has no edges at all, and every year it gets a little further from what it was for.

He said: your grandfather came one more year after it was forbidden. He was eighty-six. He stood at that gate with the lamp and eleven men behind him who were all committing an offence, and it was not the same and he knew it was not the same and he came anyway, because a man who has one door does not stop going through it when they take the sign down.
Then he said: and then he had a year with no Muharram in it.
I said: what?

He said: 1375. First time in fifty years. Nemat went up to Mirdamad on the bus to fetch him and your grandmother said he was asleep, and he was not asleep. He was sitting in the courtyard with a screwdriver. Nemat stood in front of him for a full minute. Your grandfather asked him, very politely, whether he had come about the machine.
He said: and he died in Aban of the next year.
And then Agha Sadegh, who was a very old man and not a clever one and had no framework for any of this, said the following, and it is the single most devastating sentence anybody has ever said to me:
I have never known whether that was the reason or whether I am an old fool who needs it to be a reason.

I am thirty-four years old and I hold a professional qualification in a country eleven thousand kilometres from that corridor and I have read a certain amount about all of this in a second language. I have read what the doctors say happens to a brain like his, and I know that it does not need a reason, and that it would have happened to him in a yard with the lamp in his hand exactly as it happened to him in a courtyard with a screwdriver.
And I still do not know either.

That is the position. It does not improve. There is a man who had one scheduled hour a year in which he was permitted to be what he actually was, and the hour was taken away for good reasons, and two years later he did not know his own son, and there is no way on earth to run the other version and see.
There is one more thing and then I will leave him alone.

Agha Sadegh said: on the last one, in 1374, when it was already forbidden and already behind the gate, your grandfather brought you to the corner of the street and left you with the baker’s boy and went in for twenty minutes with the lamp and came out and took you back up on the bus.
He said: you were six.
He said: you have almost certainly seen that gate before.
I have gone over this ten thousand times and I have no memory of it. None. I have a smell of machine oil and three other things and that is the entire inventory.
But when I stood at the mouth of that alley at five in the morning on Ashura in the year 1382, before I knew anything at all, before I had a single fact —
I knew which gate it was.
I have told myself for nineteen years that this is because I had been floating over it for six years and had memorised the paint.
That is one explanation. It is the small ugly one and it is probably true and I am supposed to prefer it.
And on certain nights, in another country, with two hands that ache before rain, I do not prefer it.
35. THE PLAIN — the road to Shaam
Now I have to go back over it again, because the last part of this story has different people in it and most of the people you have learned are dead.
So. Quickly, from the top, the way the rowzeh-khan does it on the eleventh night when the yard is half empty and everybody’s voice is gone.

Hossein, grandson of the Prophet, refused a pledge to Yazid and left Medina. He was turned off the road at Karbala on the second of Muharram. On the seventh they cut him off from the river. On the tenth, after three days without water, every male in his camp was killed. His brother Abbas died in the river bed with a punctured waterskin. His son Ali Akbar, eighteen, and his nephew Qasim, thirteen. His infant son Ali Asghar, held up to be seen, shot through the throat. And Hossein himself, alone, in the last hour.
The tents were burned.
Who is left.
Zaynab, his sister, in her fifties.

Zayn al-Abidin, his son, twenty-two or twenty-three, so ill he cannot stand, and the only adult male alive because of it. He is the fourth Imam. Everything that our half of Islam has after this point comes down through a man who survived because he was too sick to be worth a sword.
Roqayyeh and Sakineh and the rest of the children, whose names are given differently in different books.
And that is the entire remainder. Women, children, and one man with a fever.
They were tied.
The captives were roped and put on camels without saddles and marched first to Kufa — the city that had written twelve thousand letters — and then, over weeks, to Damascus. Which we call Shaam
[SHAAM].

That is a distance of about eight hundred kilometres. In the accounts the heads went ahead of them on the spears, so that the people of each town came out to look at the heads first and then, a little behind, at the family walking.
Zaynab walked into the court at Kufa with a rope on her and the governor Ebn-e Ziad said to her, from the seat, how did you find what God did to your family?
And she said: I saw nothing but beauty.

Then she took the room apart. In front of the governor, in front of the guard, roped, a fifty-year-old woman four weeks after watching her brothers and her nephews and her sister’s children killed in front of her, and she spoke for long enough and well enough that he ordered her stopped.
She did it again in Damascus, in front of Yazid himself, with the head of her brother in a dish on the floor of the room.
I want to say what that actually accomplished, because it is the reason there is a black banner on my street.
Yazid won on the tenth of Muharram. Completely. Militarily it is not even an event — a garrison force annihilated a party of seventy-two, and it took an afternoon.
And then he made one mistake, which was to march the survivors through every town between Iraq and Syria, and let them be looked at, and let them talk.
By the time they reached Damascus the story had been told out loud, by an eyewitness, in every market square on eight hundred kilometres of road.
Within four years there were risings. Within sixty years the dynasty was gone.
He killed everyone who could fight and left alive the two people who could speak.
That is what Zaynab is for. That is why she is in every yard in this country every year. Not because she suffered the most, although she may have. Because she is the one who went and told.
The men are why we mourn.
She is why we still know.
36. THE PLAIN — the court at Shaam
They came into Damascus in the morning, because that was arranged. You do not bring a thing like that into a capital at night.

Some weeks of road behind them. The heads went first on the spears, a day ahead, so that each town’s population had already been out and looked and formed an opinion by the time the family walked through.

And Damascus — Shaam — was decorated. That is in the accounts and it is the detail that tells you what was believed to have happened. The city was hung with cloth. There were drums. People had come out into the streets in the good mood of a public occasion, because what had been announced was a victory over rebels, and a victory is a holiday.
So the women and children of the Prophet’s family were walked through a celebration.
Yazid held court and had them brought in.

Understand the arrangement in that room. He is on the seat. The room is full — courtiers, officers, foreign guests, and the accounts specifically mention an ambassador from Byzantium, which matters, because it means the caliph was showing something to a foreign power.
On the floor there is a dish, and in the dish there is the head of Hossein.
And Yazid, who was a poet as well as a caliph and could not resist a gesture, took a cane and tapped it against the teeth.
Now.
I said earlier in this book that Zaynab is why we still know, and I said it quickly, and I owe it a chapter.
Here is her position, precisely.

She is somewhere in her fifties. Four to six weeks ago she watched her brothers, her nephews, her sister’s children and her own two sons killed in a single afternoon. She was in a tent that was set on fire. She has walked eight hundred kilometres roped, through towns, being looked at. She has been robbed of everything including the cloth she covers herself with, which in her world is not theft, it is a specific and deliberate humiliation.
She has no status. She has no protector. Every adult male of her family is dead except one who is standing behind her with a fever, in chains, aged twenty-two.
She is, in the exact and technical sense of the word this book keeps circling, ghariba [gha-REE-beh]. The feminine of gharib [gha-REEB]. A stranger. A person with nobody obliged to come.
And she is standing in front of the most powerful man on earth, in his own hall, in front of his court and a foreign ambassador, with her brother’s head in a dish on the floor.
Yazid says something to her. In one version he quotes poetry. In another he says something about God having humiliated them.
And in Kufa, weeks earlier, Ebn-e Ziad had said the thing that gets quoted most: how did you find what God did to your family?
And she had said: I saw nothing but beauty.
I want to spend a moment on that sentence because a new reader will hear it as piety and it is not piety, it is a counter-attack.

He has framed the afternoon as a verdict. God did this to you; therefore God has judged you; therefore we are correct. That is the whole imperial argument and it is the argument every winner in history has made.

And she takes it and turns it over. If this was God’s doing, then it was not yours. You did not defeat anybody. You were the instrument of something that was already written, and my family walked into it knowing, and they are exactly where they intended to be, and you are standing in a room congratulating yourself for being used.
She did it in one line, roped, in front of the man who could have had her killed for it in the next second.
Then in Damascus she spoke at length.
I am not going to reconstruct the speech, because there are versions and I do not trust myself with them and because the content is less important than the physics.

What she did was this. She stood in the hall of a government that had just, at enormous political cost, produced a story — that a rebel was put down — and she told a different story to the only audience in the world that could not be prevented from hearing it. The court. The officers. The visitors. The people who would go home and repeat it.
She named what had been done to the children. She named the three days without water. She said, in front of the foreign ambassador, exactly what he had brought into that room in a dish.

And she said — and this is the sentence that ended a dynasty on a delay of sixty years — something to the effect of: plot as you like and strive as you like, and you will never erase our memory, and you will never kill our revelation.
Yazid ordered her stopped.
That is the moment. Not a battle. A man in the strongest position any human being occupied in that century, in his own hall, on his own day of victory, having to tell a roped woman to stop talking.
Because he had realised, four sentences too late, that the room was listening.

And what did it accomplish. This is the part I want a new reader to have, because otherwise this is just an admirable thing that happened to a brave woman a long time ago, and it is not, it is the mechanism.

On the tenth of Muharram, Yazid had won absolutely. Seventy-two dead in one afternoon by a professional army. There was nobody left to raise a flag and no claim left to press and the file was, by any military assessment, closed.
Then he made one decision. He decided to display them.

He marched the survivors through every town between Iraq and Syria and put them in front of crowds, and then put them in his own court in front of his own officers, because a victory is not real until it is seen.
He held them up to be looked at.

And in doing it he gave the only two people who could still speak — a woman in her fifties and a sick young man — an eight-hundred-kilometre stage and a guaranteed audience in every market square on the route.

Within four years there were risings in his name’s despite. Within a decade there was a war. Within sixty years the dynasty was in the ground, and the family he had annihilated in an afternoon had become the permanent moral opposition of half of Islam, and is still, thirteen hundred years later, the reason a street in south Tehran goes black in winter.
He killed everyone who could fight.
He kept alive, roped and displayed, the two people who could tell it.

Zaynab lived. Somewhere between one and two years, most accounts say, though some give longer. She got the survivors home. She is buried either in Damascus or in Cairo and both cities are certain and I am not going to adjudicate.
And this is what she is for, and why every yard in this country weeps for her and not merely about her.
The men in this story are what happens when you decide to die.
She is what happens when you are not permitted to.
They were killed in an afternoon and it was terrible and it was, for them, finished by sundown.
She had to get up the next morning.
And the morning after that.
And walk.
PART FIVE — THE YARD
37. THE NIGHT — the tenth, dusk, the green gate

Between the nazri and the start of the tenth night there is a gap of about an hour when the street is at its emptiest, because everybody has gone home to change or to lie down for twenty minutes, and the light in Esfand at that hour goes a colour I have never been able to name. Not orange. Something under orange.
I go back to the alley.
I do not have a plan. I want to be clear about that, because later everybody assumed I had a plan, and a fifteen-year-old does not have a plan, a fifteen-year-old has a direction.
The alley is exactly as it was at five in the morning, except that now there is a light on above the green gate. A bare bulb in a wire cage, the kind you put over a yard door.
I stand in front of it for a while. Then I do the stupidest and bravest thing I have ever done, which is knock.
An old man opens it.
Not old like Agha Sadegh. Old like a wall is old. Seventy-something, in a vest and a jacket over it, holding the gate at the edge with two fingers.
He looks at me. He looks at my collar, which is black and wrecked, and at my hands, which are empty.
And his face changes in a way I have seen maybe four times in my life. It is the face of a man who has been waiting for something for a year and has just heard it arrive.
He says: you’re Shabani’s boy.
And I say yes. Because I am. It is my grandfather’s name, and my father’s, and mine, and nobody has said it to me like that, in a doorway, in six years.
And he says: no. Not tonight.
And he starts to close the gate.
And I put my hand on it.
I want to describe what was behind him, because I got about four seconds of it and I have kept those four seconds the way you keep a photograph.
A yard, smaller than ours. Concrete. A washing line with nothing on it. A wooden bench against the far wall.
And on the wall above the bench, at head height, a row of nails, and on the nails, hanging by their grips, a row of shrouds — white, folded, laundered, the way you would hang aprons in a kitchen.
Underneath them on the bench, in a line, wrapped in cloth, in the shape that objects that length are always the shape of.
Six of them.

And the old man saw me looking, and he did not hurry, and he did not slam it. He put his hand flat on my chest, very gently, the way you would move a child away from a stove, and he pushed, and I went back one step, and the gate closed.
Through it he said: go and ask your uncle.
38. THE PLAIN — the eleventh day
The bodies were left where they were.

That is the eleventh day. The army left on the eleventh, taking the captives and the heads, and they did not bury anyone, and they had ridden the horses over the field, and so what was left on that ground was not a set of bodies, it was a field.
For three days nothing happened.

Then a local tribe called the Bani Asad [BA-nee A-sad], who lived in a village nearby and who had taken no part in any of it and who had spent three days deciding, came out onto the plain and buried them.

They did not know who was who. That is the detail that finishes people. They were burying seventy-two men who had all been decapitated and then trampled, in the open, three days into it, in Iraq. There is a tradition that they could not identify a single one until Zayn al-Abidin came back later and walked the ground.
They dug and they put them in and they put a mark on it.
And that mark is now a shrine with a gold dome that four million people walk to on foot every year.
There is one more thing about the eleventh and I am going to say it here because I have never been able to put it anywhere else.

The Bani Asad were not heroes. They were a village. They watched an army come, and they watched it camp, and they watched it cut a family off from the river for three days within walking distance of their homes, and they watched the smoke go up off the tents on the tenth.
And then they waited three days, until the army was definitely gone, and then they came out and did the decent thing.
Everybody in this story who is not in the tents is either standing in the crescent not wanting to be the one, or standing in the village waiting for it to be over so they can be helpful afterwards.
That is not a criticism. That is a description of almost everyone who has ever lived. It is certainly a description of every man who was in that alley.
39. THE NIGHT — the tenth, the eleven minutes
Mehran is sitting on the floor of the front room with his back against the wall and the light off, which is where he sits when it is bad.
I say: who was in the alley.
He does not ask which alley.
That is the answer, right there. I got the whole thing before he said a word, because a man who does not ask which alley is a man who has one.

He talks for a long time. It costs him. Every four or five sentences he has to stop and get organised and I sit there and let him and do not offer him anything, because at fifteen I had decided that this was cruelty and it was the only cruelty available to me.
Here is what he said, in the order he said it, without the gaps.
Sohrab Ayeneh did not go to Dubai.

Sohrab was twenty-four. He had a voice that made a yard of four hundred men into one man. He had been the maddah of Heyat-e Bani Fatemeh since he was twenty-one and he had carried the alam for six years before that and through it, which is to say he had played Abbas six times, which is to say the green cloth on my shoulders last night had been on his shoulders and had gone back into the trunk with him still in it, and nobody had told me because there is no way to tell a boy that.
And every year, before dawn on Ashura, Sohrab went to a yard behind a green gate with about a dozen other men and did the forbidden thing.
Last year the cut went wrong.

Not deep. Mehran was very insistent about that and I have thought about why. It was not deep. It was a scalp cut like the others, in the wrong place, a centimetre or two off, into something that was not supposed to be there or was bigger than it was supposed to be. Mehran used the word sharyan. Artery.
And the head bleeds the way a head bleeds, and a scalp artery does not close, and Sohrab went down on the concrete with his head lower than his feet because the yard slopes to the drain.
There were eleven or twelve men in that yard.

Every single one of them was, at that moment, committing an offence. Not a small one. Not a parking matter. There is a ruling from the top of the country that says this is forbidden, and there are twelve men in a yard at four in the morning with blades and shrouds, and one of them is on the ground.

If you call an ambulance, an ambulance comes with a crew and a form and a question, and behind the crew comes everything else. Every man in that yard has a family. Two of them have shops with licences. One of them is a schoolteacher. One of them is the son-in-law of the man who owns the yard.
Mehran said: nobody decided to let him die. I want you to understand that. Nobody said the words. Not one man in that yard said we should not call.
What happened was that they discussed it.

They stood in a yard and discussed it, and they were reasonable, and they raised good points, and somebody said what about Tajrish, we could drive him, and somebody said which car, and somebody went to get the car, and somebody else said wait, if we move him it gets worse, and somebody said pressure, hold pressure, and they held pressure.
And Mehran — who had been at Majnoon, who had carried men, who was the only person in that yard who had ever put his hands inside anybody — Mehran was the one they turned to.
And Mehran said: wait.

He said it because he thought the bleeding was slowing. He said it because in his experience the ones you move are the ones you lose. He said it because he was thirty-five years old with a third of a set of lungs standing in the cold at four in the morning and everybody in the yard was looking at him and he had eight seconds.
Eleven minutes.
He knows the number because there is a clock on the wall of that yard, an ordinary kitchen clock, and he looked at it when Sohrab went down and he looked at it again when it was obvious.
And then he said the thing I have carried longest, and it is not about him.
He said: you want to know what actually killed him.
I said yes.
He said: it was not the blade and it was not the artery and it was not me saying wait.

He said: it was that every man in that yard, including him, including me, had come to believe that what was happening on that concrete at four in the morning in Nazi Abad was the same event as what happened on a plain in Iraq thirteen hundred years ago. Not like it. The same. Continuous with it.
He said: and a man who thinks he is standing in a holy afternoon does not think about arteries.
He said: Sohrab went deeper than he had ever gone and he was not being brave and he was not showing off. He was being accurate. He was trying to get the resemblance right.
And Mehran, on the floor, in the dark, with a third of a set of lungs, said:
He was accurate about the wrong thing. And so were we, for eleven minutes, standing round him doing theology.
Then he said the thing that has run underneath every conversation I have had since.
He said: and the terrible part, Ali, the part you will not understand until you are older, is that I still do not know if I was wrong.

He said: maybe he was gone in the first minute. Maybe an ambulance in four minutes does nothing. Maybe I made the correct clinical decision in a yard at four in the morning and he died anyway and the only thing I actually did wrong was live afterwards.
He said: I have had one year to find out and there is no way to find out. That is what it is. It is not guilt. Guilt would be a relief. It is a question that does not close.
And he laughed, and the laugh went into the other thing, and I did not look at the wall this time.
I said: and Dubai?
And he said: somebody said it. In the yard. Before the sun came up. Somebody said he’s gone to Dubai and it went round the room like a plate and by six in the morning it was a fact.
I said: everybody knows?

He said: everybody who needs to. That is about eleven families. And their wives. And after that it stops being a secret and becomes something else, which is worse, because a secret is a thing people are keeping and this is a thing people are not saying, and there is no lock on it and nobody guarding it and it holds better than any secret ever held.
I said: his mother?
And Mehran looked at the floor for a while.
And he said: his mother makes the nazri. She’s been in the yard behind Nemat’s shop every year of your life. She was at the pot yesterday.
40. THE PLAIN — the one who lived
Zayn al-Abidin was twenty-two or twenty-three and he had a fever so bad he could not stand up, and that is the entire reason there is a religion for me to be standing in.
Think about the arithmetic of that.

Every adult male in that camp made a decision on the ninth night with the lamp out. Seventy-two of them chose to stay and every one of them was killed for it. And the line — the whole line, everything that comes after, every Imam, every shrine, every black banner on my street in the year 1382 — comes down through the one man who was too ill to make the decision at all.

He did not choose. He was not brave. He was in a tent with a fever, and when they set the tents on fire they had to be told to leave him, and the tradition says it was Zaynab who stood in front of him and made them.
And then he was roped and put on a camel and walked eight hundred kilometres to Shaam with his family’s heads on spears ahead of him.
He lived another three and a half decades.
There are two things preserved about the rest of his life and they are the only two things I need.
The first is that he wept. Constantly, and for decades, and it is not embarrassed about this in the sources, it is recorded almost as a job title. He is one of the ones who weeps. Thirty-four years.
The second is that he did not talk about it. What he did instead was write prayers. Whole books of them, and they are still read, and they are about almost everything except that day.
A man survived the single worst afternoon in the history of his family, and then spent three decades weeping and writing about other subjects.
I did not think anything at all about that when I heard it, on the tenth day of Muharram in 1382, standing in a yard with my back stuck to my shirt.
I have thought about very little else since.
41. THE NIGHT — the tenth night
Six hundred people. The gate open, the passage full, men on the wall, men on the flat roof of the shop with their legs hanging over.

It is the last night. Everybody’s voice is gone. That is part of it — by the tenth night nobody in that yard can produce a clean note, and so the sound of the tenth night is six hundred ruined throats, and it is uglier and better than any other night of the year.
I am at the front.
I have been at the front since I was nine.
I want to describe the machine properly now, because I spent nine days inside it thinking it was weather.
The speech goes about forty minutes and it is flat on purpose.
The rowzeh goes about thirty and it builds and then stops the moment the room breaks.

Then the slow section. Latmiyeh. Open hand, once every second and a half, maybe slower, and it goes on for a long time — longer than you would think anyone could stand, twenty minutes, twenty-five — and what it is doing is getting six hundred separate men breathing on the same interval. That is all. It is not music. It is respiratory alignment.
Then the shoor comes in and the beat roughly doubles.
And the beat does not vary.

That is the thing I had never once noticed in six years, because it is like noticing your own pulse. The zakir puts Hossein into the delay unit and the delay unit is set, and it does not drift, and it does not accelerate the way a drummer accelerates, and it holds absolutely flat for two hours.

You cannot breathe irregularly inside that. It is not possible. Your chest is being hit on the beat by your own hand and everyone around you is doing it and the man on your left is close enough that you can feel his arm and if you fall out of time you strike him.
Two hours. On no food since dawn, on no sleep since the night before that, in minus four, in the tenth day of a ten-day accumulation.
I go out at about the fortieth minute of the shoor.
And this time it is different, and I know why now, and the reason is that for the first time in six years I went into it knowing something.
The boy below is in the first row, on the left, three metres from the shop door, and his hands are moving and his mouth is moving and he is not in there.
The crowd is one animal, breathing on the beat.

And above the yard, above the tarpaulin, above the shop roof with the men’s legs hanging over it, the whole of the neighbourhood is laid out and it is all going at once — our dasteh in the yard, and another one three streets north on the main road, and the loudspeakers on the mosque, and every one of them is on a slightly different beat, and it sounds like several machines in one factory.
And the alley is in the middle of it. The alley is dark. Nobody is in it. There is a bulb on above the green gate.
And it is not the desert. It has never once been the desert.

Six hundred men below me are weeping for a plain in Iraq thirteen hundred years ago and I am the only person in this neighbourhood who has been hovering over a drain in a side street for six years calling it Karbala, and the reason I am the only one, the reason nobody else is up here, the reason this does not happen to Agha Sadegh or my uncle or the man on my left —
— is that it does not happen to anybody.
I came back so hard that I was sick on the carpet.
They took me into the shop.

Two men under the arms, through the door, past the block, into the back where the sawdust is, and they sat me on a crate and somebody put a glass of tea in my hand with four sugars in it, and the noise from the yard came through the wall like weather.
And then everybody left, and Haj Nemat closed the door.
He sat on the other crate. He is a big man and he sat with his forearms on his knees and his hands hanging.
He said: how long have you known?
I said: since this morning.
He said: which part.
And that was when I understood that there were parts.

He told me. He did not defend himself and he did not soften it and I have to say, having had nineteen years to be angry about that night, that the way he did it was the only decent thing available to him by then.
He said: you were nine.

He said: your grandfather had been dead six months. Your mother had taken you to her sister in Karaj for a month and brought you back the same. You had stopped speaking. Not shy. Stopped. Six weeks of nothing, and then five months of the least a child can get away with, not to your uncle, not to a doctor, nothing you did not have to.
He said: and I put you at the front of the dasteh on the first night of Muharram because I did not know what else to do with a child who would barely speak.
He said: and on the eighth night you went down and came back up and you were talking. You talked for two hours. You would not stop.
And he said: so I kept you at the front.
Then he told me the rest, which took about four minutes and unmade my entire life.
He said: your chains are light. Sadegh gives you the light one. He has given you the light one since the first year.
He said: you are at the front because the front is where the delay unit is loudest and where the beat is cleanest, and at the back the beat arrives late off the wall and it drifts.

He said: I do not let you eat on the ninth and tenth. You think you are fasting. You are not fasting, there is no fast in Muharram, there has never been a fast in Muharram. Your uncle and I agreed it when you were ten.
He said: I keep you up. The night before Ashura I always find you something to do.
And he said the thing about the beat.

He said: Sohrab used to run the shoor at about a hundred and forty. Fast. That is the fashion, that is what the young men want, that is what fills a yard. And in the second year I noticed you did not go under at a hundred and forty. You went under at a hundred and twenty-nine.
He said: so I asked him to hold it at a hundred and twenty-nine. Not a hundred and thirty. A hundred and twenty-nine.
And then Haj Nemat, a butcher, fifty-six years old, in the back of his own shop, said the following sentence, and I have carried it across an ocean:
Four hundred and sixty-five thousandths of a second between one beat and the next. That is your number. I have known your number since you were ten years old.
I said: why.
And he said: because when you go under, the yard fills.
He said it flatly. He did not dress it.

He said: a boy who leaves his body is a sign. A sign brings people. People bring money. Money fills three cauldrons that feed four hundred families for two days and pays for the tarpaulin and the generator and Agha Sadegh’s rent, which he does not know I pay.
He said: I am a butcher and I run a heyat and both of those are businesses and I have never once pretended otherwise to God.
And I said — and I was fifteen, and my throat was destroyed, and I had been sick on a carpet in front of six hundred people, and this is the only thing I could get out:
I said: so it isn’t real.
And he looked at me.
And he said: I did not say that.
He said: I said I know the number.
42. THE NIGHT — what the butcher called me

There is a thing that happened in the first week of the first year that I did not understand at nine, could not have understood, and that I have not been able to put down anywhere in this book until now because until now you did not have the word.

It was Farvardin, not Muharram. That is worth saying. My uncle brought me south in the spring, a month before any of it, because a paediatrician in Jordan Street had run out of things to try and because he had asked my mother for a week.

We went into the shop for meat. That is all it was. My uncle needed meat and the man he bought meat from was Haj Nemat Qorbani, and I was nine and standing by the door not saying anything, which is what I did then.
And Haj Nemat came round the block wiping his hands and looked at me for slightly too long.
And he said, to my uncle, but loudly enough that it was for me:
So this is the crystal.
I did not react. I had not reacted to anything for five months.
But my uncle put his hand flat on the counter, which is a thing he did, and did not say anything for a while, and then said something about the meat.
I did not think about it again for six years.

Six years. I was in that man’s yard sixty nights. He put me at the front of a procession and gave me a light chain and a part in a play and held a drum machine at a specific number for me, and in all of that time he never used the word again, not once.

And then on the tenth night of 1382, in the back of that shop, on a crate, with a glass of tea in my hand and four sugars in it and my throat destroyed, he told me he had known my number since I was ten, and I said so it isn’t real, and he said I did not say that.
And I got up to go. And at the door I turned round and I said:
Who told you to call me that?
And he did not ask me what I meant.
He said: your grandfather.

He said: every year for as long as I have had this shop. He came down before it was light and he stood at the yard gate with the lamp, and after seventy-three at the other one, and afterwards he sat in this shop and drank tea with me while it got light, because the first bus back up was at seven and because an old man does not go straight home from a thing like that.
He said: so he sat there. Where you are sitting.
He said: and he talked about you.
I said: about me.

And Haj Nemat, who was a butcher and a treasurer and a man who had run a boy at a hundred and twenty-nine beats a minute for six years, said the following, and this is the last thing in this book I am going to be able to write without stopping.

He said: he had his son’s two boys and he was proud of both and he talked about the older one the way men talk about a boy who is easy. Football. School. Girls, later. He talked about Amir the way you would talk about good weather.
He said: and then he would say, and the little one.
He said: and something happened to his face.

He said: he told me you would not smile at anything. He said it like it was the funniest thing in the world and he said it every year. He said, that child looks at me as though I have personally disappointed him and he is deciding how to break it to me.
He said: and he called you Boloor. In here. To me. To Sadegh. To men you have never met, who are still alive, who are in that yard tonight.
He said: for four years I have known the name of a child in the north of this city who never smiled.
And then he said: and then in Aban somebody came in and said Abbas Shabani was gone. Not from the family. From the family we heard nothing. From a man who drove a taxi.
He said: and I stood exactly where I am standing now.
And he said: and I thought, the crystal.
I want to be accurate about what that did to me, because it is the reason the next morning happened.

Everything I had been told that night — the chains, the front row, the fast that was not a fast, the four hundred and sixty-five thousandths of a second — all of it I had heard as a machine. I had been operated. That is what I understood at half past ten on the tenth night of Muharram: that I was a device that a butcher had learned to switch on.
And then at the door he said the crystal, and the whole thing turned over in one second.

Because the man who ran the machine had been sitting in a shop at seven in the morning for four years listening to my grandfather be helplessly, stupidly, boringly in love with a child who would not smile at anything.
He had not been given a device.

He had been given the little one. The one the old man used to talk about after. He had been handed the thing that man loved most in the world on an afternoon in Aban when there was nothing else left to do about it, and he had put him at the front where he could see him and made the chain light so it would not hurt him and given him the only part in the whole story where a boy gets his hands on the thing he wants and puts it back.
And he had done it for six years and had never once said the name out loud, because the name belonged to a dead man and Nemat did not think it was his to use.

That is not a defence of him. He also filled a yard with me and paid Sadegh’s rent with the takings and knew it and said so and did not apologise, and every word of that is true at the same time and does not cancel.
But I went out of that shop understanding, for the first time in my life, that the two things were not in competition.
He was using me and he loved me, in the same movement, with the same hands, and there was no seam in it anywhere, and there never had been, and there is not one in me either.

And at half past four the next morning I went into that storeroom and lifted the felt and took my grandfather’s chain out of the bottom of the trunk, and I want to say now, at thirty-four, on the record, that I did not go to the green gate to hurt myself.

I went because a man in a shop had said a word out loud that nobody had said since I was nine, and I wanted, more than I have ever wanted anything before or since, to go to the one place on earth where my grandfather was still a person, and where my father, who had got one syllable of that word out in a doorway and stopped, had once been a boy.
43. THE PLAIN — the story will not stay where I put it
On the eleventh of Muharram the army left and took the captives and the heads, and the bodies were left in the open on the plain, and for three days nothing —

For three days nothing happened, because the men who had been there were reasonable men with families and shops and licences, and they stood in the yard and discussed it, and somebody said Tajrish, and somebody said which car —
No.
Start again.

On the eleventh of Muharram the army left, and a village called the Bani Asad waited three days until it was definitely over and then came out and did the decent thing, and they could not tell one man from another because of what had been done to the field, and so they buried seventy-two men without names and put a mark on it.
And the mark is a gold dome now.

And there is a bulb over the green gate and there is a drain in the middle and the ground slopes to it and the concrete around it is a paler colour where the hose reached and darker where it did not, in a shape like a hand with the fingers spread, and nobody has put a mark on it, and nobody is going to.
That is what happened to the story on the tenth night of Muharram in the year 1382.

I had been given it in order, one piece a night, for ten nights, the way it is given to every child in this country. Medina, the road, Karbala, the seventh, the ninth night with the lamp out, the river, the infant, the last hour, the horse, the road to Shaam.

And I had kept it in a separate drawer from my own life, which is what the drawer is for, which is the entire purpose of the drawer, which is why we have a story from thirteen hundred years ago instead of just crying about our own dead.
And on the tenth night the drawer came out of the front of the cabinet and everything went on the floor together.
I could not tell it any more without the alley in it.

I still cannot. I am thirty-four years old and I have told the story of Karbala to the woman I live with, in English, in a country where nobody knows what a heyat is, and when I got to the eleventh day I stopped in the middle of a sentence and had to say I would finish it tomorrow.
Every day is Ashura and every land is Karbala.
They put that on a banner and hang it over a street and everyone walks under it for a thousand years, and nobody, not one person, considers that it might be a threat.
PART SIX — THE STRANGERS
44. SHAAM-E GHARIBAN
There is no track any more. There is one night and it happened twice.
The word first, because everything is in the word.

Shaam is evening. It is also, spelled the same and said the same, the name of Damascus, which is the city they were marched to, and I do not think anybody planned that and I have never met an Iranian who has not noticed it.

Ghariban [gha-ree-BAAN] is the plural of gharib, and gharib is the word the whole thing turns on, and it does not translate. The dictionaries say stranger. That is not wrong and it is nowhere near enough.

A gharib is not somebody you do not know. A gharib is somebody who is far from their own people. It carries the whole apparatus underneath it: that a person alone is a person unprotected, that in the world this word comes from there was no such thing as an individual with rights, there was only a person with relatives, and that when you say a man died gharib you are not saying he died sad, you are saying he died with nobody obliged to come.
We use it for the exile. We use it for the migrant. We use it for the man buried in a country where the writing on the stone is in the wrong alphabet.

And on the night of the tenth of Muharram, we use it for a group of women and children sitting on burnt ground in the dark with every man they were related to lying unburied within a hundred metres of them.
The evening of the strangers.
Here is what that night was.

By late afternoon on the tenth it was finished. The army had taken the heads. They rode the horses over the field. Then, because a camp is loot, they went through the tents — and this is the part that is always told quickly and should not be — they took the cloth off the women’s backs. Not as an assault, as an inventory. They took earrings out of ears. There is a line in the old accounts about a soldier crying while he robbed a child, which is either the truest sentence in the whole of it or somebody’s late addition, and I have never been able to decide, and I am not sure it matters.
Then they set the tents on fire and left, and the survivors ran out of the burning into open ground, in the dark, in October, on a plain.
Around fifty children. Some women. One man, Zayn al-Abidin, with a fever, unable to stand, dragged out because Zaynab stood in the way.

No tents. No water — still no water, that had not changed, the river was still there and still not theirs. No men. And the field they were sitting in the middle of was not a field any more, it was where everyone they knew was lying.
And the tradition preserves what Zaynab did, and it is not a speech, and it is not brave, and it is the reason this night is different from every other night of the ten.
She counted them.

In the dark, by touch. Going from child to child, putting a hand on a head, saying a name and waiting for an answer. Because the fire had scattered them and the horses had scattered them and she did not know how many she had.
Some of the names did not answer. She had to go and find those.
And there is one more, and every Iranian knows it and it is the single hardest thing in our entire year.
There was a small girl. The books give her name differently and mostly she is called Roqayyeh and she was three or four years old.
She had not been told. Nobody had had the time to tell her, or nobody could.
So she went across that ground in the dark, on the night of the tenth, from one body to another, looking for her father.
That is the story. That is all of it. It is four seconds long and it has held a country for thirteen hundred years.
Now the other night.
By eight o’clock the yard is unrecognisable.

They take the bulbs out. Not switch off — take out, unscrew, so nobody can put them on again by reaching for the wrong thing. The generator is off and the silence where the generator was is the first thing you notice, because it has been running for ten days and you did not know you were hearing it.

The speakers are down. The microphone is coiled and put in the box. The delay unit is off and unplugged at the wall, and that detail, on that specific night, in that specific year, is going to matter to me for the rest of my life.
No dohol. No sanj. No zanjeer.
Nobody stands.

They roll the carpets out flat and everybody sits down on the ground, which is the first time in ten days that anyone has been below anyone else, and the yard that has been a formation for ten days becomes a room.
And then they bring the candles.
The children carry them. That is fixed. It is not that the children are permitted to, it is that it is theirs, and no adult takes it from them.

They come in through the gate holding them low in cupped hands against the wind, in a line, eighty or ninety small candles, and they set them down on the concrete and on the flat of the carpets and along the top of the wall and around the rim of the empty cauldrons.
Some of them float them. A shallow bowl of water with a candle in it, and the flame moves when anyone walks past.
And that is the light for the rest of the night. That is all of it. Six hundred people in a walled yard in the dark with ninety candles on the floor.
It looks like what it is meant to look like, which is a plain with fires on it and nobody left to guard them.
Nobody performs.

I need to be clear about how strange that is, after ten days. For ten days everything has had a shape. There has been a man with a microphone and a beat and a formation and a set of instructions for your body. And now there is a yard full of men sitting on the floor in the dark, and there is no beat, and there is nothing to do with your hands.

The old rowzeh-khan does not use the microphone because there is no microphone. He sits on the carpet like everybody else and he speaks at the volume of a man in a room, and the men at the back cannot hear him properly and nobody asks him to speak up.
He tells the counting. He tells the small girl.

And the yard comes apart in a way it has not come apart in ten nights, and it is completely different in kind from the other nights, and this is the thing I most want to explain to somebody who has never sat in it.

For ten nights, six hundred men weep in time. On the beat. In a rhythm, in a formation, striking their own chests in unison, and there is something in that which is almost comfortable, because a grief with a tempo is a grief that is being managed. You are not falling. You are being carried.
On Shaam-e Ghariban [shaam-eh gha-ree-BAAN] there is no tempo.
And so what you hear in that yard is six hundred men crying out of time with each other, and it is a horrible sound, and it is the truest sound I have ever heard human beings make.

Here is what is actually happening in that yard, and this is the part that is never said out loud, and it is the reason this night is the one Iranians come back for even when they have stopped coming back for anything else.
Nobody there is crying about a plain in Iraq.
I said that earlier, in a different chapter, about a different night, and I was guessing. On Shaam-e Ghariban it is not a guess, it is the design.
This is the night the country puts its own dead down on the floor.

Look at what is in front of you. A dark yard, no music, candles set on the ground, everyone sitting, everyone allowed to weep as long and as loudly and as badly as they like, and nobody permitted to comment. There is no other occasion in our lives that provides this. A funeral is three days and then you are supposed to manage. A grave is a place you go alone. Here is one night a year, guaranteed, in the calendar, where a grown man in a country that does not allow grown men very much can sit on a carpet in the dark among six hundred people and cry about his own brother, and everybody will assume he is crying about a child on a plain in Iraq, and nobody will ever ask.
The story is the cover.

That is not cynicism. That is the engineering. The story is thirteen hundred years old and enormous and belongs to no one family, and because of that it is strong enough to carry every private death in the neighbourhood on top of it without anybody having to admit what they are carrying.
Every man in that yard has smuggled somebody in.
And it is much older than Islam, and Mehran told me this that night, sitting on the carpet beside me with a candle between his shoes, in a voice like a door in the wind.
He said: you know we were doing this before.

He said: there was a prince called Siavash [see-yaa-VASH]. Long before any of this. He was innocent — that is the whole of him, he is the innocent one — and he was accused of a thing he had not done, and he walked through a fire to prove it and came out the other side clean, and then they killed him anyway. In another country. Far from his own people. They put him down over a basin so as not to spill his blood on the ground, and where a drop got out anyway a plant came up.

He said: and the people of this country mourned him. Every year. With their faces cut and their hair cut and singing. Two thousand years ago there was a place in Bukhara [bo-khaa-RAA] where they did it and the historians wrote it down and complained about the noise.
He said: and then Karbala happened, and we already knew how to do this. We already had the movements. We had been rehearsing for a thousand years.
And then he said — and I would like it understood that this is a thirty-six-year-old man with ruined lungs sitting on the floor in the dark:
He said: Ali jan, we are the only people on earth who were ready.
I go and find Agha Sadegh at about eleven.
He is sitting with his back against the wall near the storeroom door, out of the candles, in the actual dark, which is where he has put himself.
I sit down next to him.
I say: it’s the eleventh.
He looks at his watch, which he cannot read, and then at the sky.
He says: near enough.
And he tells me about Sohrab, and it is not the same story Mehran told me, because Mehran told me what happened and Agha Sadegh tells me what it was.
He says: he carried the alam six years. He was better at it than anyone I ever gave it to. He had a way of taking it down the carpet slowly enough that you thought he was going to stop.
He says: I gave him the light one too.
I say: what?

He says: the chains. Sohrab’s was light. From the first year. I gave it to him for six years. Your grandfather’s was not. Eleven years on a heavy one, before your father was born, and then I gave him the lamp.
And I sit there in the dark next to a man past eighty and I say: is anybody’s chain heavy?
And Agha Sadegh laughs. Actually laughs, in the dark, on Shaam-e Ghariban, one small dry sound.
He says: about half. The other half are ones somebody was worried about.
Then he says the thing I came for and I did not have to ask.
He says: I am going to tell you why we all lied to you. Not Nemat. Nemat has his own reasons and he told you them tonight and I heard about it from three men before you sat down.
He says: I lied to you.

He says: when you told me about the alley on the seventh night, I knew exactly what you were describing before you had finished describing it, because I have been in that yard before dawn every year since before your father was born, and behind that green gate since seventy-three.
He says: and I put my hand on your neck and I told you it was Karbala.
And I say: why.
And he says:

Because you were fifteen, and you had just been shown, from the air, a thing that eleven grown men have not been able to look at directly in a year. And I had about two seconds. And in two seconds an old man reaches for the thing that has always worked.

He says: every land is Karbala is true. That is the terrible part. I did not tell you a lie. I told you the truest sentence we have, in order to stop you from asking a question, and that is a worse thing than lying and I have known it since the seventh night and I have not slept.
We sit there for a while.
Then he says, and this is the last thing anybody says to me before everything goes wrong:
He says: your grandfather’s chain is still in the trunk. Bottom left, under the felt, with green tape on the grip.
He says: forty-odd years. I never gave it to anybody else.

He says: and if you go into that yard tomorrow, Ali, they will not stop you. That is what nobody has told you. They are not guarding it. There is no lock on it. There has never been a lock on any of it.
He says: the only thing standing between you and that gate for six years has been a lot of tired men making sure you were somewhere else.
The candles go down one by one over about two hours and nobody relights them and that is deliberate too.
By one in the morning there are maybe fifteen left. By two there are four.

Six hundred people sitting in a walled yard in south Tehran in the dark in winter, and nobody has spoken for a long time, and somewhere near the gate a woman is making a sound that I now know was Sohrab’s mother, and every man in that yard knew it too, and not one of them turned round.
That is Shaam-e Ghariban.
Everyone knows. Nobody turns round. The candles go out on the floor.
And in the morning there is one more day.
45. THE NIGHT — the eleventh morning
The trunk is not locked. Agha Sadegh told me that and he was telling me something larger and I heard only the small thing.

I go into the storeroom at about half past four in the morning on the eleventh of Muharram and I lift the felt and the chains are in there in a heap like something asleep, and at the bottom on the left there is one with green tape wound round the grip, and the tape has gone hard and brown at the edges, and it comes away from the pile heavier than the others.
Substantially heavier. I had not understood how much until my hand took the weight of it and dropped four inches.

I stand in a dark storeroom holding a thing my grandfather used for eleven years and would not let anybody else use for forty, and I am fifteen years old and I have not been asleep and I have not eaten since the day before yesterday and there is a number in my head — four hundred and sixty-five thousandths of a second — going round like a wasp in a jar.
I do not take the chain to hit myself with. I want that understood, because everybody afterwards assumed that, and it is not what it was.
I took it because it was his, and because I was going to a place he had gone, and because at fifteen you do not go anywhere important empty-handed.
It is minus five. The banners are still up, and they will come down on the thirteenth, and for two more days they hang over a street where nothing is happening.
The alley has the bulb on. It has probably had the bulb on all night.

And the gate is open. Not ajar. Open, hooked back against the wall, the way you open a gate when men are going to be coming through it in ones and twos before dawn and you do not want the sound of a latch on a quiet street.

They are already in there. Nine of them. There is a hurricane lamp on the bench and the shrouds are down off the nails and three men have them on already, white, over the black, tied at the waist, and one of them is helping another one with the knot the way you help a man with a tie.

And they are talking quietly about something completely ordinary. That is the thing I did not expect and have never got over. About a road closure. Two men in shrouds at five in the morning discussing whether Navvab is shut.
The old man from the gate sees me first.
He says my grandfather’s name. Not to me. Out loud, to the yard, like an announcement, like a warning at sea.
And every man in that yard turns round.
What happened next took about eleven seconds and I have had nineteen years to slow it down and it will not slow down.
I came in. I got about three metres. I had the chain in my right hand hanging down and I was not swinging it and I was not going to.
And they came at me. Not one. Four or five, at once, from both sides, and they did not shout, because the entire architecture of that yard is that nobody shouts.

A hand on my chest. A hand on the back of my collar. Somebody’s forearm across me. And I did the thing a fifteen-year-old does when four grown men take hold of him, which is fight, badly, and I got an arm free.

The ground is concrete and it is wet because they had hosed it, because they hose it before as well as after, and it is minus five, and there is a film of ice on it in the places the light does not reach.
Three of us went down together.

And one of the men going down was one of the men in a shroud, and he had a qameh in his hand, because he had been holding it when he turned round, because he had been holding it the way you hold a spoon.
Nobody swung anything. I want that on the record, permanently, in a book, because for nineteen years people have looked at my hands and constructed something.
I went down forward with both hands out in front of me the way every human being on earth goes down.
And the blade was on the concrete between us, edge up, because it had come out of his hand when he fell.
That is all. That is the whole event. It is not a rite and it is not a punishment and it is not a martyrdom and it is not a suicide and it is not, in any way at all, interesting.
I put both palms down on a knife lying on the floor.
The left one is a diagonal across the fat of the palm below the thumb, about six centimetres, deep enough that I did not feel it for four or five seconds and then felt it in my teeth.
The right one goes across the base of all four fingers, which is worse, and which is why my right hand does what it does in cold weather.
Both hands, at once, in a yard, in the dark, during a prevention.
Abbas lost both arms carrying water to children who never got it.
I lost the use of two tendons falling over on a wet floor while being stopped from doing something I had not thought about for longer than ninety minutes.
That is the resemblance. That is what a resemblance is. It is the closest thing available.
46. THE NIGHT — the eleventh day
Nine men in a yard at five in the morning, all of them committing an offence, and a bleeding fifteen-year-old on the floor.
You already know the shape of this. You have already read what this room does.
They called it in eleven seconds.
The old man was the one. He said one word — a name, somebody’s name, one of the younger ones — and then he said car, and then he said now, and the yard emptied of any discussion at all.

Two of them took the shrouds off and threw them over the wall into the next yard rather than spend two seconds folding them. Somebody put the qameh down a drain, and the drain is the drain, and I heard it hit.
Somebody wrapped my hands in a shroud, which is the only genuinely poetic thing that occurred that entire month and nobody in that yard noticed they were doing it.

And I was in a Paykan on the way to Loghman [logh-MAAN] with my hands up in the air over my head and a man I had never met in my life sitting beside me holding my wrists up and saying, over and over, in the tone of a man reading out a football result: he fell on a knife in his uncle’s kitchen. He fell on a knife in his uncle’s kitchen. Say it back to me.
I said it back to him.
I have said it back to a great many people since.

Fourteen stitches in the right, nine in the left. A tetanus injection. A doctor of about thirty who looked at my hands and then at my face and then at my hands, and asked me three times, in three different ways, each time more gently.
And on the third time he sent the man out of the room to do it.
And there was a gap of about two seconds before I answered him, and I know exactly what was in it, and I have never told anybody.
What was in it was Abbas.

Four hours. That is the interval. Four hours after a blade lying on a wet floor had opened both my hands during a scuffle that had no meaning of any kind, a man in a coat asked me a straight question in a well-lit room, and the first thing my mind reached for — before the truth, before the lie, before my mother, before anything — was a man in a river in Iraq with his arms gone.
I did not say it. I want that on the record. I have that much.
But I want it on the record too that it was still there, and that it was still the very first place I went, and that it was not even close.

That is what the thing does. It does not leave because you have found it out. Finding it out is nothing. I had known for eleven hours that the alley was concrete and that the number was a hundred and twenty-nine, and I lay on a trolley in Loghman with my hands in the air and reached for the desert anyway.
And I said: I fell on a knife in my uncle’s kitchen.
And he looked at me for a while and then wrote it down.

I have thought about him more than about almost anybody else in this story. He is the only person in the entire month who tried, straightforwardly, with no rite and no story and no thirteen hundred years behind him, to give me an exit. He had about ninety seconds and he used all of them.
And I looked at a man who was offering me a way out, and I refused it, and I did it in front of witnesses, in daylight, with the paper right there.
I did exactly what Abbas did. I would like to be able to say it felt the same.
Haj Nemat came at eleven in the morning.
He did not sit down. He stood at the end of the bed with his coat still on and his hands at his sides and he looked at the dressings for a long time.
And then he said: I have three things to tell you and then I am going to go, because if I stay I will say more than three.
He said: the first is that I am not sorry about the number. I am not going to stand here and be sorry about it. It fed people.

He said: the second is that I did not know Sohrab was going to die and I did not know your grandfather was going to go the way he went and both of those are things I say to myself at three in the morning and they are both true and neither of them helps.
And then he said the third one, and it took him a while to get to it, and he said it looking at the wall.
He said: why do you think I gave you Abbas.
I did not answer.

He said: I have been putting boys in that play for twenty-six years. Do you know what part I give a boy I am worried about? Not Ali Akbar. Not Qasim. Every boy in this neighbourhood wants Qasim because he gets to die at a wedding.

He said: I give him Abbas. Every time. Because Abbas is the only part in the entire story where a boy stands in front of four hundred people, gets his hands on the thing he wants most in the world, and puts it back.
He said: I have watched you rehearse putting it back for nine days.
He said: it was the best I had.
And then he went, because he had said three things.
Agha Sadegh died in the summer of that year. He was eighty-one. It was nothing to do with any of this.

The last thing he ever said to me was in the hospital corridor about a week after, and it was not profound, and I am going to put it here anyway because he was in a hurry and he was old and he said the true thing instead of the good one.
He said: I should have given you the heavy one.
I said: what?

He said: the first year. You were nine. I should have given you a heavy chain and let you find out what it costs, and you would have put it down after twenty minutes and you would have been a boy who tried it once.
He said: we made it easy for you for six years and then we were surprised you did not know it was hard.
47. THE PLAIN — Safar, and the road
The mourning does not stop on the tenth. That is the thing nobody outside tells you and the thing everybody inside forgets to mention.

Muharram is the first month. The next month is Safar. And the mourning runs on into it, and it does not finish until the fortieth day, which is called Arba’een [ar-ba-EEN], which is simply the word for forty.
Forty days after Ashura, the survivors — Zaynab, and the sick son, and the children — are said to have come back through Karbala on their way home from Shaam, and to have stopped at the ground.
That is what is being marked. Not a death. A return to a place by the people who were dragged away from it.

Millions of people walk to it now. On foot, across Iraq, in a line that takes days. It is possibly the largest annual gathering of human beings on the planet and almost nobody outside our part of the world has heard of it.
And Safar, the name of the month, is also a word.
It is one of those words that does two jobs in the same mouth and everyone knows it and nobody remarks on it. Safar is the second month of the Islamic year.
Safar also, in Persian and in Arabic, simply means a journey.
You mourn through Muharram. And then the month you go into, the month you are still mourning in, the month you are still not finished in, is called Journey.
They built the leaving into the calendar. Thirteen hundred years ago. It is the next thing after the tenth night and it always has been.
I left on the twenty-eighth of Ordibehesht [or-dee-be-HESHT], 1389, which is May of 2010, from Imam Khomeini airport at ten past four in the morning.
I was twenty-one.
Mehran was dead by then — the winter of 1387, and it was the lungs, and it took eleven days, and I was there for all eleven and I am not going to write about it here.

The paperwork took two and a half years and cost more than I have ever earned in a year since. There were affidavits. There was a sponsor. There was a lawyer in Vanak with a photograph of his son in a graduation gown.
There is one thing I had worked out by then and it is the only thing I took with me that was worth anything.

I had not stopped believing it. I want to be exact, because people in this country assume that a man who leaves a thing like that has seen through it, and I have never seen through it, and I do not expect to.
What I stopped doing was locating it.

That is the whole of what I learned, and it took six years and both hands. The story is not a map. It was never a map. There is no alley in it and no drain and no gate, and if you find one you have not been shown something, you have made an error, and the error will feel exactly like grace, every time, for the rest of your life.

It is a container. It is thirteen hundred years old and it is enormous and it belongs to nobody, and that is precisely why it can hold what will not go anywhere else — a brother, a marsh, a son, an old man with a lamp who at the end could not find the gate. It works. It has worked for a very long time on a very large number of people and I am not going to stand here and be clever about it.
The only rule is the one nobody says out loud, because nobody in that yard has ever needed to.
You must never once mistake the container for the address.
And I believed, on the twenty-eighth of Ordibehesht 1389, standing in that queue with a bag, that I had got myself out.

I want to be exact about that. I did not think I was lucky. I thought I had done it. I had spent six years being a boy that a street had arranged around itself and I thought that the one thing in my life that was mine, unmanaged, unassisted, chosen, was that I had put myself on a plane.
Haj Nemat came to the airport.

He did not say much. He never said much. He shook my hand — the right one, which by then closed about eighty per cent, and he took it carefully, the way everybody in that neighbourhood took it, without ever once mentioning why.
He gave me a plastic bag with bread in it, because that is what people do, and then he said, God protect you, and then he said one more thing.
He said: don’t go to a heyat over there.
I laughed. I actually laughed at him, in an airport, at four in the morning.
I said: Haj Agha, they don’t have heyats in California.
And he looked at me for a second too long.
And he said: they have everything everywhere.

There are, depending on how you count, somewhere between eleven and twenty places in greater Los Angeles where the ten nights are observed. Within a few years I knew where nine of them were, without ever once looking.
It took me eleven years to stand in one. On the tenth night, in August, at ninety-four degrees, at the back, in a country where nobody knew what my hands were.
I did not take a chain.
And that is where the second part of this starts.

But on the twenty-eighth of Ordibehesht 1389 I did not know any of that. I went through the gate and I found my seat and the plane went up over the city at about half past four, and Tehran at that hour from the air is orange and enormous and does not end.

And somewhere down in it, three streets from a bakery, there is an alley a metre and a half wide with a drain in the middle and a bulb over a green gate, and the concrete around the drain is a paler colour in a shape like a hand with the fingers spread.
And nobody has put a mark on it.
And in about eleven years, when I finally understand who paid the lawyer in Vanak, I am going to sit down on the floor of a kitchen in another country and understand that I did not leave.
I was moved.
The way you move a boy to the front of a procession.
Because you love him, and because it is the best you have, and because you have never once, in the entire arrangement, thought to ask.
GLOSSARY

Persian and Arabic terms, place names and figures appearing in this book. Phonetics are given as plain English syllables, with the stressed syllable in capitals. alam [a-LAM] — Arabic, a sign or standard. The battle standard carried in a mourning procession, usually brass or steel and topped with an open hand. Abbas carried the standard at Karbala, so the alam stands for Abbas.
aman [a-MAAN] — Arabic, safety, quarter. A written guarantee of protection. Shemr brought one to Karbala naming Abbas and his three full brothers, and Abbas refused it.
Arba’een [ar-ba-EEN] — Arabic, fortieth. The fortieth day after
Ashura, marking the end of the mourning period. Millions walk to
Karbala on foot for it.
Ashura [aa-shoo-RAA] — Arabic, from ’ashara, ten. The tenth day of
Muharram, on which Hossein was killed.
