Ayeneh [aa-yee-NEH] — Persian, mirror. A family name.
bay’at [bey-AT] — Arabic, pledge of allegiance, performed by placing one’s hand into the hand of the man being pledged to. Yazid’s demand for Hossein’s bay’at begins the story.
Boloor [bo-LOOR] — Persian, crystal; the bright, light-catching kind, used of chandeliers and cut glass.
dabirestan [da-bee-res-TAAN] — Persian. Iranian high school, following rahnamayi.
dasteh [das-TEH] — Persian, a bunch, a group held together. A mourning procession.
deeg [DEEG] — Persian. A very large cooking cauldron, used for communal votive food.
dohol [do-HOL] — Persian. A large double-headed drum carried in processions.
Esteghlal [es-tegh-LAAL] — Persian, independence. One of Tehran’s two great football clubs; blue. The historic rival of Persepolis.
gharib [gha-REEB] — Arabic, stranger. Not someone unknown, but someone far from their own people and therefore unprotected — a person with nobody obliged to come. Feminine ghariba
[gha-REE-beh]; plural Ghariban [gha-ree-BAAN].
gheimeh [ghey-MEH] — Persian. A stew of split peas, meat and dried lime, cooked in bulk and distributed during Muharram.
heyat [hey-AT] — Arabic, a body, a shape, a form. A neighbourhood mourning association: a street’s grief organised into an institution, with a treasurer, a storeroom and a membership.
hoor [HOOR] — Arabic and Persian. The marshes of southern Iraq and south-western Iran.
hosseinieh [ho-sey-nee-YEH] — Persian. A hall built for the mourning of Hossein.
Hurr [HORR] — Arabic, free. The cavalry commander who blocked
Hossein’s road, and who changed sides on the morning of Ashura.
latmiyeh [lat-mee-YEH] — Arabic, from latm, to strike. The slow chest-beating section of a mourning night.
maddah [mad-DAAH] — Arabic, from madh, praise. The lead reciter who sings the elegies.
Majnoon [maj-NOON] — Arabic and Persian, mad, possessed. The name of the lover in the old poem of Majnoon and Leyli, and also of the marshland oilfield contested throughout the Iran–Iraq war.
mashk [MASHK] — Persian. A water carrier made from a whole sewn animal skin.
Muharram [mo-har-RAM] — Arabic, forbidden. The first month of the
Islamic year, one of four in which fighting was traditionally prohibited.
nakhl [NAKHL] — Persian, palm tree. A wooden bier carried in procession, shaped after the palm said to have borne a body.
nazr [NAZR] — Arabic, a vow. A private undertaking made to God, requiring no clergy, no witness and nobody’s permission. nazri
[naz-REE] is the food distributed in settlement of it, which may not be sold and may not be refused to anyone.
nowheh [now-HEH] — Arabic, from nawh, wailing; the cry of a dove.
The sung lament of a mourning night, performed in call and response.
pardeh [par-DEH] — Persian, curtain. A large painted narrative canvas showing the whole Karbala story, unrolled and revealed a section at a time by a travelling narrator.
Persepolis [per-se-PO-lis] — Tehran’s other great football club; red.
Historically dominant in the south of the city and among the bazaar.
qameh [gha-MEH] — Persian. A short heavy single-edged blade.
qameh-zani [gha-meh-za-NEE] is the practice of striking the scalp with it, formally forbidden in Iran in 1994.
qorbani [ghor-baa-NEE] — Arabic, from the root q-r-b, nearness. A sacrifice; literally an act of drawing close.
rahnamayi [rah-na-maa-YEE] — Persian. Iranian middle school, three years, ending at about fourteen.
rowzeh [row-ZEH] — Persian, garden. From Rawzat al-shuhada, “The

Garden of the Martyrs,” written in Herat in 1502; the book’s title became the word for the telling of the Karbala story itself. Recited by a rowzeh-khan [row-zeh-KHAAN]. Women’s gatherings are rowzeh-ye zananeh [row-ZEH-ye za-naa-NEH].
sabil [sa-BEEL] — Arabic, a road, a way. A free water station set out in the street for whoever is passing.
Safar [sa-FAR] — Arabic. The second month of the Islamic year, through which the mourning continues. The same word means a journey.
sanj [SANJ] — Persian. Large hand cymbals used in processions.
Saqqa [sagh-GHAA] — Arabic, water-carrier. The title of Abbas, named after the errand he failed.
Sarasari [sa-raa-sa-REE] — Persian, nationwide. The examination formerly sat simultaneously by every third-year middle school student in Iran.
shabih [sha-BEEH] — Arabic, resembling. shabih-khani, resemblance-reading, is the older and plainer name for the Karbala passion play.
Shaam [SHAAM] — Arabic and Persian. Damascus, and also evening.
Shaam-e Ghariban [shaam-eh gha-ree-BAAN], the evening of the strangers, is the night after Ashura.
shoor [SHOOR] — Persian, fervour, ardour; also salty. The fast, driving final section of a mourning night.
sineh-zani [see-neh-za-NEE] — Persian. Rhythmic beating of the chest with the open hand.
sofreh [sof-REH] — Persian, a cloth spread for eating. A votive gathering dedicated to a particular figure, most often run by women in a private house.
takyeh [tak-YEH] — Arabic, a leaning-place. A building or enclosure used for mourning rites; the word was borrowed from Sufi usage.
Tasu’a [taa-soo-AA] — Arabic, nine. The ninth day of Muharram.
ta’ziyeh [ta-zee-YEH] — Arabic, condolence. The Iranian passion play re-enacting the events of Karbala. See shabih.
tumar [too-MAAR] — Persian, a scroll. The strip of paper from which performers in a ta’ziyeh read their lines aloud, so that nobody is mistaken for the person they represent.
zakir [zaa-KER] — Arabic, one who mentions. The second voice in a mourning recitation, repeating a name to hold the beat.
zanjeer [zan-JEER] — Persian, chain. zanjeer-zani [zan-jeer-za-NEE] is the practice of striking the back and shoulders with a cluster of blunt flat chains in time.
Zoljanah [zol-jah-NAAH] — The horse of Hossein, which returned to the tents without him.
